a: These are the words
p: The Hebrew name of the book is Devarim, "Words." "Deuteronomy" comes from a Greek misreading of 17:18.
b: Jews name the book from its opening, Elleh ha-devarim, "These are the words," or simply Devarim, "Words." The English title comes from the Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus. In 17:18 the king is told to write "a copy of this law" (mishneh ha-torah). The Greek rendered it to deuteronomion touto, "this second law," and the phrase became the book's name. The book is not a second, different law. It is Moses' retelling and explaining of the covenant to a new generation. The rabbis also called it Mishneh Torah, "the repetition of the Torah," for the same reason. The book is mostly speech: three long addresses by Moses (1:6–4:40; 5:1–28:68; 29:2–30:20), then his song, his blessing and his death.

a: on the far side of the Jordan
p: The phrase means east of the Jordan, as seen from the land of Israel. Readers have asked who was speaking from the west.
b: Moses never crossed the Jordan, yet the narrator calls his position "beyond the Jordan," the way a person living in Canaan would. The KJV tried to soften this with "on this side Jordan." The medieval Jewish scholar Abraham ibn Ezra hinted that a few such phrases were added after Moses, and called this "the secret of the twelve." Many later scholars took the phrase as a sign that the narrator wrote from inside the land. Others note that 'ever ha-yarden had become a fixed name for the region east of the river, like "Transjordan," and that Deuteronomy uses it for both sides of the river (3:20, 25; 11:30). Either way, the narrator's frame (1:1–5) speaks about Moses in the third person, and the speeches themselves start at 1:6.

a: between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth and Di-zahab
p: Several of these places are unknown. The rabbis read the names as quiet reminders of Israel's sins.
b: Paran and Hazeroth are known from Numbers (Numbers 10:12; Numbers 11:35), but Tophel, Laban and Di-zahab cannot be placed with confidence. The Sifre, the Aramaic Targum Onkelos and Rashi read the list as a polite rebuke: Moses names the places where Israel sinned instead of naming the sins. "Laban" (white) recalls their complaint about the white manna, "Hazeroth" recalls Korah's revolt (or Miriam's), and "Di-zahab," "enough gold," recalls the golden calf. Modern commentators treat the list as a real itinerary, perhaps joined from two sources, that marks where Israel had been. Both readings agree that the book opens by looking back over the journey before it looks ahead.

a: It is eleven days from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea by the Mount Seir road.
p: The trip from Sinai to the edge of the land took eleven days. Israel took forty years.
b: Deuteronomy usually calls the mountain of the covenant Horeb, where Exodus and Numbers more often say Sinai. The point of this aside is the contrast with the next verse: a journey of eleven days became a journey of forty years. Rashi drew the lesson plainly: Israel's sin turned a short road into a long one. Kadesh-barnea is usually placed at Ein el-Qudeirat in the northeastern Sinai, roughly 150 miles from the traditional Mount Sinai (Jebel Musa) by the desert routes, which fits an eleven-day march. "The Mount Seir road" probably means the route toward the hills of Edom.

a: In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month
p: The speeches are dated about two months before Israel crossed the Jordan.
b: The date fits the other dates of the Torah. Aaron died on the first day of the fifth month of the fortieth year (Numbers 33:38). Moses speaks on the first day of the eleventh month. After his death Israel mourns for thirty days (34:8), and Joshua crosses the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month of the next year (Joshua 4:19). So Deuteronomy fills the last weeks of Moses' life. Jewish tradition holds that Moses died on the seventh of Adar, the twelfth month, so that the whole book was spoken in about five weeks.

a: all that the LORD had commanded him
p: Where the Hebrew has God's personal name, YHWH, the Plain English writes "the LORD" in capitals.
b: The Hebrew here is the four-letter personal name of God, YHWH, probably said "Yahweh." Jews stopped saying it aloud before the time of Jesus and read Adonai, "Lord," in its place. The Septuagint wrote Kyrios, "Lord," and most English Bibles print "the LORD" in small capitals. This site does the same. "Lord GOD" (3:24; 9:26) stands for Adonai YHWH. Deuteronomy's favorite way to name God is "the LORD your God," which comes about 300 times. It ties the name to a relationship: he is the God who belongs to this people, and they belong to him.

a: Moses began to make this law clear
p: Moses does not give new laws here. He "makes plain" the teaching, which is what the word torah means.
b: The verb be'er means to make clear or to write plainly; it returns in 27:8, where the law is to be written on stones "very clearly." Moses explains and urges, like a preacher. The word torah comes from a root meaning "to point, to teach." It means instruction, guidance, teaching, and only later a law code in our sense. This site renders it "law," as most English Bibles do, but the reader should hear "teaching" in it too. In Deuteronomy "this torah" means Moses' whole address, and later the scroll that holds it (31:9, 24–26). A midrash quoted by Rashi says Moses explained it "in seventy languages," that is, for all nations.

a: Enough of staying at this mountain!
p: The Hebrew rav lakhem, "it is much for you," returns at 2:3 and 3:26, each time at a turning point.
b: Literally, "Much for you, sitting at this mountain." God uses the same short phrase when Israel has circled Seir long enough (2:3), and again when he refuses Moses' plea to cross: "That is enough from you!" (3:26). The repetition gives the first speech a shape. The people must leave the safety of the holy mountain and walk into the land; their leader must accept that he will not walk in with them. Korah's men had thrown the same words at Moses and Aaron: "Enough of you!" (Numbers 16:3).

a: as far as the great river, the river Euphrates
p: The land promised to Abraham reached the Euphrates. Israel held so much only briefly, if at all.
b: This is the largest map of the promise, the same as in Genesis: "from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates" (Genesis 15:18). Deuteronomy repeats it at 11:24, and Joshua 1:4 echoes it. The kingdom of David and Solomon is described as ruling up to the Euphrates (1 Kings 4:21), but Israel never settled that far. Some readers take the borders as a promise still to be fulfilled; others as the ideal limits of a royal claim, of the kind found in ancient treaties; others as a promise that grew with later hopes.

a: I cannot carry you all by myself.
p: Exodus credits Jethro with the idea of judges, and Numbers has seventy elders. Deuteronomy tells it as Moses' plan.
b: In Exodus 18 Moses' father-in-law sees him worn out and says, "This load is too heavy for you. You can't carry it by yourself" (Exodus 18:18). In Numbers 11 Moses cries, "I cannot carry this whole people alone" (Numbers 11:14), and God gives seventy elders. Deuteronomy blends the words of both and does not mention Jethro. Traditional readers say Moses, speaking to his people, sums up and does not need to name his source. Critical scholars see Deuteronomy retelling older stories in its own way, here to show Israel as a people who share in governing itself. Either way, the point in this speech is that Moses could not carry Israel alone, and the next verses explain why: they had grown so many.

a: Today you are like the stars of the sky in number.
p: Moses points to the promise of Genesis 15:5 and says it has come true.
b: God had told Abram, "Look toward the sky and number the stars... So will your offspring be" (Genesis 15:5; see Genesis 22:17; Genesis 26:4). Moses says the promise has been kept: a family of seventy (10:22) has become a nation too large for one man to judge. Deuteronomy will later turn the image around as a warning: if Israel breaks the covenant, the people who were as many as the stars will be left few (28:62). Moses' blessing in the next verse, "a thousand times more," shows that he does not see Israel's size as a problem, only its government.

a: I also gave your tribes officials
p: The shoterim were officers, probably record keepers, who worked beside the judges and the army.
b: The Hebrew shoterim is probably related to the Akkadian verb shataru, "to write." They appear as Israel's foremen in Egypt (Exodus 5:6), as officers who give orders in war (20:5–9; Joshua 1:10) and beside judges in each town (16:18). They were probably the people who kept lists and passed on commands. Deuteronomy lays out a whole system of public offices: judges, officials, priests, a king and prophets (16:18–18:22). Some scholars, such as S. Dean McBride, have called this the Bible's nearest thing to a constitution.

a: or the foreigner who lives with him
p: The ger, a foreigner living in Israel, gets the same justice as an Israelite. This site calls him "the foreigner."
b: A ger was someone who had come from elsewhere and lived among the Israelites without land or clan to protect him. Older English Bibles call him "the stranger," newer ones "the sojourner" or "the resident alien." This site says "the foreigner." Deuteronomy speaks of him more than any other book of the Torah, usually beside the orphan and the widow, the people with no one to stand up for them (10:18; 14:29; 24:17–21; 27:19). Here, in the first law Moses recalls, justice for him is part of justice itself. Israel was to remember that they were foreigners in Egypt (10:19).

a: Do not play favorites when you judge
p: The Hebrew idiom is "do not recognize faces." The same idea runs to the New Testament's warnings against favoritism.
b: Literally "Do not recognize faces in judgment": do not let the identity of the person, rich or poor, friend or stranger, decide the case. Deuteronomy repeats the law at 16:19 and grounds it in God himself, who "does not play favorites" (10:17). Leviticus forbids favoring the poor as well as the great (Leviticus 19:15). The Septuagint's Greek wording lies behind the New Testament words for "favoritism," used of God in Acts 10:34 and Romans 2:11 and of the church in James 2:1–9.

a: the judgment is God's
p: Judges do God's work. A wrong verdict is not just bad government; it is an offense against God.
b: Because judgment is God's, a judge has nothing to fear from powerful people and everything to fear from God. King Jehoshaphat told his judges the same thing: "It is not for people that you judge, but for the LORD" (2 Chronicles 19:6). In 17:8–13 the hard cases go to the priests and the judge "at the place the LORD will choose," which takes the place of Moses' role here. The Sifre adds that a judge who takes money from one side "steals" from God.

a: Then all of you came to me
p: In Numbers God orders the scouts. In Deuteronomy the people ask for them and Moses agrees.
b: Numbers 13:1–2 begins, "The LORD spoke to Moses: Send men to scout out the land." Here the idea comes from the people. Rashi joins the two: the people asked, and God let Moses send them. Many modern readers think each book tells the story for its own purpose. Numbers shows God testing his people. Deuteronomy shows that the people's own doubt was at work from the start: they wanted the road checked before they would trust the one who had promised to lead them (1:30–33).

a: They came to the Valley of Eshcol
p: Eshcol means "cluster." The scouts named the valley after a huge bunch of grapes.
b: Numbers tells the story: "They came to the Valley of Eshcol, and from there they cut down a branch with a single cluster of grapes" (Numbers 13:23). The valley lay near Hebron, still famous for its vineyards. Deuteronomy keeps only the fruit and the scouts' first verdict, "the land... is good" (1:25), and leaves out the report about the giants until the people repeat it (1:28). The word "good" for the land runs through the whole book (1:35; 3:25; 4:21–22; 6:18; 8:7–10).

a: The LORD hates us.
p: The people turn God's love inside out. Deuteronomy answers: he brought you out because he loved you (7:8).
b: The Hebrew reads "in the LORD's hatred of us he brought us out." It is the exact opposite of what Moses will teach: "It was because the LORD loved you... that the LORD brought you out" (7:8). The same doubt is put in Egypt's mouth in 9:28: "because he hated them, he brought them out to kill them." The people's complaint "in your tents," out of sight of Moses, became a byword; Psalm 106:25 repeats it. Fear of the giants grew into a belief that God himself was their enemy.

a: And we saw the Anakim there too!
p: The descendants of Anak lived around Hebron. To the scouts they were giants.
b: Numbers 13:33 has the scouts say, "There we saw the Nephilim, the descendants of Anak... In our own eyes we were like grasshoppers." Deuteronomy shows that the fear of the Anakim spread to the whole nation (1:28; 9:2). Joshua later drove them from Hebron and the hill country, leaving some in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod (Joshua 11:21–22), the Philistine towns from which Goliath later came. The Egyptian Execration Texts, curses on enemies written about the 19th–18th centuries BC, name rulers of a people called "Iy-anaq," which some scholars link to the Anakim, though the link is debated.

a: the way a man carries his son
p: God carried Israel through the wilderness the way a father carries a small son. Acts 13:18 echoes the Greek of this verse.
b: Moses had complained that he was not Israel's father, asked to carry them "the way a foster father carries a nursing baby" (Numbers 11:12). Here he says God himself did it. Hosea uses the same picture (Hosea 11:1–3), and Isaiah has God carry Israel from birth to old age (Isaiah 46:3–4). Paul's sermon in Acts 13:18 uses the Greek of this verse. Manuscripts of both Acts and the Septuagint are split between two words that differ by one letter: etrophophorēsen, "he carried them like a nurse," and etropophorēsen, "he put up with their ways." The KJV follows the second in Acts ("suffered he their manners").

a: you did not trust the LORD your God
t: The sin at Kadesh was unbelief
p: The root word is the one behind "amen" and "faith." Hebrews makes this failure the classic warning.
b: The Hebrew ma'aminim comes from 'aman, "to be firm, to rely on," the root of "amen" and of the verb used for Abraham's faith in Genesis 15:6. Numbers 14:11 has God ask, "How long will they not believe in me?" Psalm 106:24 uses the same verb: they "did not trust his word." Hebrews 3:16–19 reads the whole wilderness story through this verse: they could not enter "because of unbelief." Deuteronomy's point is the same. The problem at Kadesh was not the size of the enemy but the people's refusal to rely on the God who had already carried them.

a: because he followed the LORD fully
p: The Hebrew idiom is "he filled after the LORD." It means he followed with no holding back.
b: The phrase mille' acharei YHWH is used only of Caleb and Joshua (Numbers 14:24; Numbers 32:12; Joshua 14:8–9, 14). A related idiom describes Solomon's failure: he "did not follow the LORD all the way" (1 Kings 11:6). The land Caleb "walked on" was Hebron, the town of the Anakim he had not feared (Joshua 14:9–14). Deuteronomy names only Caleb here and gives Joshua his own place two verses later, as Moses' successor.

a: Because of you the LORD was angry with me as well.
p: Deuteronomy says Moses was shut out "because of you." Numbers says it was for his own act at Meribah.
b: Three times Moses says that God refused him "because of you" (1:37; 3:26; 4:21). Numbers 20:12 gives a different reason: Moses and Aaron "did not believe" and did not treat God as holy at the water of Meribah, and Deuteronomy 32:51 agrees with that. Readers explain the difference in several ways. (1) Moses' own sin at Meribah was provoked by the people, so both are true (Psalm 106:32–33). (2) Moses, in a speech of rebuke, stresses the people's share. (3) Many critical scholars think Deuteronomy 1–3 keeps an older tradition in which Moses suffers for the people, as a leader bound to his generation. Dennis Olson and others have read it as a kind of suffering on behalf of others. Notice that the verse sits inside the story of Kadesh, not Meribah, as if Moses shared the doom of that generation.

a: Make him strong
p: Moses is told to make Joshua strong. The word chazaq becomes the refrain of Joshua's whole commissioning.
b: The verb chazzeq, "make strong," returns when God tells Moses to "Make him brave and strong" (3:28). Moses then tells Joshua himself to be strong and brave (31:7, 23), and God repeats it to Joshua three times after Moses' death (Joshua 1:6–9). The repetition marks a handing on of leadership that runs across the end of the Torah into the next book. "Who serves you," literally "who stands before you," is a court phrase for a personal attendant (Exodus 24:13; Exodus 33:11).

a: your children who do not yet know good from bad today
t: Too young to know good and bad
p: The words echo the tree of knowing good and evil. Here they mean children too young to be responsible.
b: The generation counted at Sinai, twenty and older, is condemned; the children are spared. "Not knowing good and bad" describes young children, as in Isaiah 7:15–16, where it marks the years before a child can choose. The phrase recalls "the tree of knowing good and evil" (Genesis 2:17). Some Jewish and Christian readers took it from this verse that God does not hold young children guilty for choices they could not make. Some rabbis set the age of responsibility for such judgment at twenty, from Numbers 14:29. The parents' excuse, that the children would "become plunder" (Numbers 14:3, 31), is turned back on them: the children are the ones who will possess the land.
r: Genesis 2:17; Genesis 3:5; Numbers 14:3; Numbers 14:29–31; Isaiah 7:15–16; Jonah 4:11

a: by the road to the Sea of Reeds
p: The Hebrew Yam Suf means "Sea of Reeds." Here it probably means the Gulf of Aqaba, east of Sinai.
b: English Bibles since the Septuagint usually say "Red Sea." The Hebrew yam suf means "sea of reeds" or "sea of rushes," and this site renders it that way throughout the Torah. The name covers more than one body of water. At the exodus it was a sea at Egypt's edge (Exodus 13:18; Exodus 15:4). Here and in 2:1 the road to the Yam Suf leads south and east, toward the Gulf of Aqaba, as in 1 Kings 9:26, where Solomon's ships sail from Ezion-geber "on the shore of the Sea of Reeds." The people are sent back the way they came, away from the land.

a: You thought it would be easy to go up into the hill country.
p: The Hebrew vattahinu occurs only here. It may mean "you treated it lightly" or "you were eager."
b: The verb vattahinu appears nowhere else in the Bible. The KJV guessed "ye were ready." Many interpreters connect it with an Arabic word meaning "to think something easy," which fits the context: after refusing to go when God was with them, the people rush off to fight lightly armed in confidence, when God is no longer with them (1:42). Rashi took it from hinneni, "here we are," as if the people said, "We are ready!" The point is clear whatever the exact meaning: too-late obedience is another form of disobedience.

a: They chased you the way bees do
p: Bees chase an intruder in a swarm, far from the hive. The image is of a rout.
b: The Amorites came out like disturbed bees, in numbers, angry, and ready to chase their enemy a long way. The same image appears in Psalm 118:12 ("They swarmed around me like bees") and Isaiah 7:18, where God whistles for Assyria "like bees." In Numbers 14:45 the attackers are "the Amalekites and the Canaanites who lived in that hill country"; Deuteronomy, as often, uses "Amorites" as a general name for the peoples of the hills.

a: all the way to Hormah
p: Hormah sounds like cherem, "the ban." The place where Israel was beaten later became the place of its first victory.
b: The name Chormah comes from the same root as cherem, a thing "under the ban," devoted to destruction. Israel's defeat here, in a war God had forbidden, is set against Numbers 21:1–3, where Israel vows to put the Canaanite towns under the ban, wins, and names the place Hormah. The town lay in the northern Negev, perhaps at Tel Masos or Tel Halif; the site is uncertain.

a: all the days that you stayed there
p: The Hebrew is vague on purpose: "as many days as you stayed." Tradition says nineteen years.
b: The phrase repeats itself, a Hebrew way of saying "for as long as it was." In Numbers 20:1 Israel is back at Kadesh in the first month of a later year, and 2:14 says thirty-eight years passed from Kadesh to the Zered Valley. The rabbinic chronology Seder Olam, followed by Rashi, says Israel spent nineteen years at Kadesh and nineteen more wandering around Seir. Many modern readers think Kadesh was Israel's base for most of the forty years, with an oasis that could support it.

a: For many days we went around the hill country of Seir.
p: Thirty-eight years shrink to a single sentence. Deuteronomy tells almost nothing of the wandering itself.
b: Numbers gives the wilderness years a few stories and a list of camps (Numbers 15–19; Numbers 33:19–36). Deuteronomy passes over them in one line: "many days" circling Seir, the hill country of Edom south and east of the Dead Sea. Only in 2:14 does the reader learn how long it was. The silence fits the speech's purpose. Those were years of waiting for a generation to die, and Moses moves straight to the moment when God says, "You have gone around this hill country long enough" (2:3).

a: your relatives, the descendants of Esau
p: Israel must treat Edom as kin. In Numbers, Edom refuses Israel passage; here Israel goes around peacefully.
b: The Hebrew calls them "your brothers," because Esau was Jacob's twin (Genesis 25:24–26). Deuteronomy later forbids Israel to "abhor an Edomite," because "he is your brother" (23:7). Numbers 20:14–21 tells how Edom said, "You will not pass through," and Israel turned away. Deuteronomy describes Israel passing "by" Edom and buying food (2:6, 29). Some readers harmonize the two: Israel skirted Edom's heartland and traded with Edomites along the edge. Others think Deuteronomy follows a different route tradition. Archaeologists debate whether Edom was a settled kingdom before about the 8th century BC; surveys in the Faynan copper district show large-scale activity there already in the 11th–10th centuries.

a: because I have given the hill country of Seir to Esau as his own
t: God gives land to other nations too
p: Edom, Moab and Ammon hold their lands as gifts from the LORD, just as Israel will.
b: Three times in this chapter God protects the land of another people: Edom (2:5), Moab (2:9) and Ammon (2:19). The same verb "give" and the same word for a possession (yerushah) are used as for Israel's land. The asides in 2:10–12 and 2:20–23 add that these peoples, too, drove out giants before them with God's help. The God of Israel is lord of every nation's borders. Moses' song says the Most High "set the borders of the peoples" (see 32:8), and Amos 9:7 says God brought the Philistines from Caphtor and the Arameans from Kir as he brought Israel from Egypt. Paul's words in Athens make the same claim (Acts 17:26).

a: You have not lacked a thing.
p: The same verb returns in 8:9 and in Psalm 23:1, "I will lack nothing."
b: The verb chaser, "to lack," is used here for the forty years, and in 8:9 for the land where Israel will lack nothing. Nehemiah's prayer recalls it: "Forty years you provided for them in the wilderness, and they were short of nothing" (Nehemiah 9:21). Psalm 23:1 uses the same Hebrew word: "The LORD is my shepherd; / I will never be in need." Moses' point is practical. Israel has money and goods to pay Edom (2:6), and has no excuse to take by force what God has not given.

a: I have given Ar to the descendants of Lot as their own
p: Moab and Ammon descend from Lot, Abraham's nephew. Ar was a Moabite town or region near the Arnon.
b: Genesis 19:37–38 says the older daughter of Lot "bore a son and named him Moab," and the younger "named him Ben-ammi. He is the ancestor of the Ammonites." Their land is protected because of Abraham's kin, even though 23:3–6 bars Moabites and Ammonites from Israel's assembly for other reasons. Ar (also in 2:18, 29; Numbers 21:15, 28) seems to name a city or district of Moab on the Arnon; its location is not known for sure. The Moabite king Mesha's inscription of about 840 BC shows that the region north of the Arnon was still fought over centuries later.

a: The Emim used to live there.
p: Verses 10–12 and 20–23 read like footnotes about who lived in the land before.
b: These verses break off God's speech to give background, as ancient historians such as Herodotus did when describing a land. They are put in parentheses in this translation, as in most modern versions. They tell of tall early peoples, the Emim, Rephaim and Zamzummim, and of the Horites in Seir and the Avvim near Gaza, each replaced by newcomers. The Emim and Rephaim are linked with the war of the kings in Genesis 14:5, where Chedorlaomer struck down "the Rephaim... the Zuzim... the Emim." The asides make a point: Moab, Ammon and Edom took their lands from giants by God's gift, so Israel can do the same.

a: People also counted them as Rephaim
p: Rephaim names an ancient people of giants, but also the shades of the dead. Ugaritic texts use the same word.
b: In these chapters the Rephaim are an old, tall population east of the Jordan, of whom Og was the last (3:11, 13). But elsewhere in the Bible repha'im means the ghosts of the dead in Sheol (Isaiah 14:9; Isaiah 26:14; Psalm 88:10; Proverbs 9:18). Texts from Ugarit in Syria, from about 1200 BC, speak of the rpum as dead kings and heroes honored in rituals. Many scholars think the two uses are connected: the Rephaim were heroes of a vanished past, and so also the honored dead. Some traditional readers keep the meanings separate. Elsewhere (Genesis 14:5; Joshua 12:4) the Septuagint calls them "giants"; in Deuteronomy it keeps the name Rephaim.

a: just as Israel did in the land the LORD gave them to possess
p: The aside looks back on Israel's taking of its land as a past event, though Moses speaks before it.
b: Since Moses is speaking east of the Jordan, the phrase "as Israel did" seems to look back on the conquest of Canaan. Some take it as referring to the land already taken from Sihon and Og (2:24–3:17). Others, from Ibn Ezra on, see it as one of a few notes added by a later hand, like "to this day" in 2:22 and 3:14. Conservative scholars who hold to Mosaic authorship often accept small updating by later scribes. Critical scholars see it as a sign that the book was written in the land, long after Moses. The note's purpose either way is to set Israel's conquest beside the other nations' as one example of God's rule over history.

a: thirty-eight years
p: About two years from Egypt to Kadesh, then thirty-eight more. A whole generation dies in the desert.
b: Israel left Sinai in the second year (Numbers 10:11), so the thirty-eight years from Kadesh bring the total to forty, as promised: "In this wilderness your dead bodies will fall" (see Numbers 14:29–35). The Zered Valley is usually identified with the Wadi el-Hasa, which runs into the south end of the Dead Sea and formed the border between Edom and Moab. Crossing it marks the start of the new generation's march. Paul and the letter to the Hebrews both read this death of a generation as a warning to Christians (1 Corinthians 10:5; Hebrews 3:17).
r: 1:35; Numbers 10:11; Numbers 14:29–35; Numbers 21:12; Numbers 26:64–65; 1 Corinthians 10:5; Hebrews 3:16–19

a: The LORD's own hand was against them
p: The "hand of the LORD" that struck Egypt now strikes Israel's own fighting men.
b: The phrases "the LORD's hand," "throw into confusion" and "until they were all gone" are the language of the LORD's wars against Israel's enemies (7:23; Exodus 14:24; Joshua 10:10). William Moran argued in 1963 that 2:14–16 describes an "unholy war": the generation that refused to fight for God found God fighting against it. Only when the last of them has died (2:16) does God speak again and begin the real conquest (2:17–24). Jewish tradition noticed the timing too: Rashi, following an older midrash, says that in those years God did not speak to Moses with the old warmth.

a: the Ammonites call them Zamzummim
p: Zamzummim may be a mocking sound-word for people whose speech sounded like buzzing. It is uncertain.
b: The name is otherwise unknown. Many scholars connect it with the Zuzim of Genesis 14:5, who lived in Ham, east of the Jordan. Others hear in zamzummim an imitation of foreign speech, "the mumblers," like the Greek word barbaros for people who sounded like "bar-bar." The Hebrew root zamam can also mean "to plot," and some rabbis read the name as "schemers." No explanation is certain.

a: the Caphtorim, who came from Caphtor
p: Caphtor is usually identified with Crete. The newcomers near Gaza were the Philistines' ancestors.
b: Amos 9:7 and Jeremiah 47:4 say the Philistines came from Caphtor, and Genesis 10:14 lists the Caphtorim among peoples linked with Egypt. Egyptian texts call Crete Keftiu, and Akkadian texts Kaptara. Archaeology shows that the Philistines settled the southern coast of Canaan in the early 12th century BC as part of the movements of the "Sea Peoples," bringing Aegean-style pottery and customs. The Avvim, who lived in "villages" there before them, are named elsewhere only in Joshua 13:3.

a: This very day I will begin to put the dread and fear of you
p: The Song at the Sea had promised this: "Terror and dread fall on them." Rahab will confirm it.
b: After the crossing of the sea Israel sang, "Peoples have heard; they shake" and "Terror and dread fall on them" (Exodus 15:14–16). Moses now says the fear will start with the victories over Sihon and Og. In Jericho Rahab tells the scouts, "Dread of you has fallen on us," because the city had heard what Israel did to "Sihon and Og" (Joshua 2:9–10). The same promise returns at 11:25.

a: with an offer of peace
p: Moses offers Sihon peace even after God said to fight him. The rabbis saw here the origin of the law in 20:10.
b: God had already said, "Go to war against him" (2:24), yet Moses sends "words of peace." Rashi, following the midrash, says Moses was not commanded to do this but learned it from God, and later God made it law: "When you come near a town to fight against it, first offer it peace" (see 20:10). Modern readers ask whether the offer was sincere if God meant Sihon to refuse (2:30). One answer is that Sihon's refusal was his own, and God's hardening confirmed it. The offer itself is closely parallel to Numbers 21:22: "Let me pass through your land... We will walk on the King's Highway."

a: made his spirit hard and his heart stubborn
p: Like Pharaoh, Sihon is hardened by God. Readers have long debated what this means for his own choice.
b: The language is the language of Pharaoh's story (Exodus 4:21; Exodus 7:3), and Joshua 11:20 uses it again of the kings of Canaan. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers have usually said that God confirms or punishes a choice already made: Sihon was already hostile, and God did not stop him. Calvinist readers stress God's sovereign use of human wills for his purpose, citing Paul in Romans 9:17–18. Others read it as the Bible's way of saying that even an enemy's stubbornness serves God's plan. The verse itself gives the purpose: "to hand him over to you." This site renders qashah "hard" and the parallel verb "stubborn," as in Exodus.
orig: הִקְשָׁה... רוּחוֹ וְאִמֵּץ אֶת־לְבָבוֹ (hiqshah... rucho ve-immets et-levavo)

a: We put every town under the ban, men, women and little ones.
t: The ban: what it was and how it is read
p: Cherem meant handing over a town to God by destroying it. It is one of the Bible's hardest themes.
b: To put something "under the ban" (cherem) meant to devote it to God so that no one could use it, here by killing its people. Moab's king Mesha says the same of his war on Israel: he killed seven thousand at Nebo because he had "devoted" it to his god Ashtar-Chemosh. Readers take the Bible's ban in several ways. Some accept it as a unique judgment on Canaanite evil, limited to that time (9:4–5). Others, such as Paul Copan, argue that the reports use the stock exaggeration of ancient war accounts. Many critical scholars think the ban was more ideal than practice, a later way of saying "no compromise with idolatry" (7:2–5). Some Christian readers, from Origen on, read it as a picture of rooting out sin. See also 7:2.

a: From Aroer on the edge of the Arnon Valley
p: Aroer stood on the north rim of the Arnon gorge. The king of Moab says he rebuilt it.
b: The Arnon (Wadi Mujib) cuts a deep canyon into the plateau east of the Dead Sea, and served as the usual border between Moab and the land to its north. Aroer is the site Khirbet 'Ara'ir, on the gorge's north edge, where a fortress has been excavated. The Mesha Stele says, "I built Aroer, and I made the road in the Arnon." The phrase "and the town in the valley" is unclear; it may be a town in the gorge below Aroer, or Ar itself. Gilead is the hill country north of the Jabbok and south of it, east of the Jordan.

a: for battle at Edrei
t: Told twice, almost word for word
p: Verses 1–3 repeat Numbers 21:33–35 nearly exactly, with "we" in place of "they."
b: Numbers 21:33–35 tells the battle in the same words: "Then they turned and went up by the road to Bashan, and Og king of Bashan came out to meet them, he and all his people, for battle at Edrei." Deuteronomy turns the report into Moses' memory and adds details: sixty towns, the region of Argob, Og's bed. Edrei is modern Dera'a in southern Syria, near the Jordanian border. Bashan, the rich tableland east of the Sea of Galilee, was famous in the Bible for its oaks and its fat cattle (Psalm 22:12; Amos 4:1).

a: sixty towns, the whole region of Argob
p: Argob was a district of Bashan. Some identify it with the black lava field of the Leja in southern Syria.
b: 1 Kings 4:13 also speaks of "sixty great towns with walls and bronze bars" in Argob. Many scholars place Argob in the Leja (ancient Trachonitis), a rugged basalt plateau, though others put it farther west. In the 1800s, travelers such as J. L. Porter described the stone houses there as "giant cities of Bashan" built by Og's people. Archaeologists now date most of those standing buildings to Roman and Byzantine times. The region does have many older sites from the Bronze Age, but the sixty towns of this verse have not been identified.

a: The Sidonians call Hermon Sirion, and the Amorites call it Senir.
p: The names Sirion and Senir are known from outside the Bible. The note fits a well-informed ancient writer.
b: Mount Hermon, over 9,000 feet high, is the snowy peak at the northern edge of the land. Sirion appears in texts from Ugarit as a mountain paired with Lebanon, just as in Psalm 29:6: "He sets Lebanon jumping like a calf, and Sirion like a wild ox's young." Senir is the name of the mountain in Assyrian records of Shalmaneser III (841 BC) and in Ezekiel 27:5 and Song of Songs 4:8. In 4:48 Hermon is also called Sion (not the same word as Zion). Such notes show the book's interest in names and older peoples, as in 2:10–12.
r: 4:48; Psalm 29:6; Song of Songs 4:8; Ezekiel 27:5; 1 Chronicles 5:23

a: his bed was a bed of iron
p: Og's "bed" was about 13 feet long. It may have been a couch decorated with iron, or a black basalt coffin.
b: Nine by four cubits is about 13½ by 6 feet. The Hebrew 'eres means a bed or couch, and it can be used of a bier for the dead. Four main explanations are offered. (1) It was a royal bed with iron fittings, a rare luxury before about 1200 BC, as Alan Millard has argued. (2) It was a coffin of black basalt, which looks like iron. (3) It was one of the ancient dolmens, stone burial tables that fill the region and that some people later called "giants' beds." (4) It was a ritual bed of the kind found in temples: the Babylonian Esagila Tablet gives the bed in the shrine on top of Marduk's ziggurat, Etemenanki, as 9 by 4 cubits, the same size as Og's. The question "Is it not in Rabbah of the Ammonites?" (modern Amman) reads like a writer pointing to a famous object still on show in his own day.

a: I gave the Reubenites and the Gadites
t: The tribes east of the Jordan
p: Numbers 32 tells of a quarrel over this land. Deuteronomy presents it simply as Moses' gift.
b: In Numbers 32 Reuben and Gad ask to settle east of the Jordan because it is good for cattle, and Moses angrily compares them to the scouts who discouraged Israel. They promise to fight beside their brothers, and only then does Moses give them the land. Deuteronomy leaves out the quarrel and tells the land's division as a list of gifts (3:12–17), with the duty to fight added after (3:18–20). Some readers see Deuteronomy as a summary for a new generation; others see a different view of the eastern land, which was always a little apart from Israel's heartland (Joshua 22). The "half-tribe of Manasseh" is the clan of Machir and Jair (3:13–15).

a: Havvoth-jair, as they are still called today
p: Havvoth-jair means "Jair's tent villages." Numbers and Judges tell of Jair in different ways.
b: Numbers 32:41 says that Jair, a descendant of Manasseh, captured these villages and named them after himself. Judges 10:3–4 tells of a judge Jair from Gilead whose thirty sons rode thirty donkeys and had thirty towns "called Havvoth-jair to this day." 1 Chronicles 2:21–23 counts sixty towns, which may combine Jair's villages with the towns of Argob. "To this day" is one of the phrases that show the writer looking back over some time (see 2:12).

a: But all your strong men must cross over armed
p: Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh must lead the way across the Jordan. Joshua holds them to it.
b: The promise of Numbers 32:20–22 is restated as an order. Joshua reminds them of it on the first day of his command (Joshua 1:12–18), they cross ahead of the others (Joshua 4:12–13), and Joshua sends them home with praise when the land is won (Joshua 22:1–6). The phrase "your strong men," literally "all the sons of strength," means the men fit for war. Their families and herds stay behind in towns already taken (3:19).

a: until the LORD gives your brothers rest
p: "Rest" in Deuteronomy means peace from enemies in a settled land. Hebrews 4 reads it as pointing beyond Joshua.
b: The promised "rest" (menuchah) is a land where Israel lives safely, free from enemies all around (12:9–10; 25:19). Joshua 21:44 says the LORD "gave them rest all around," and 1 Kings 8:56 praises God for giving rest to Israel in Solomon's day. Psalm 95:11 remembers the wilderness generation who would "not enter my rest." Hebrews 4:8 argues from these texts: "If Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on," so "a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God."

a: At that time I begged the LORD for mercy.
p: This word names a weekly Torah reading. A midrash says Moses prayed 515 times, the number value of the word.
b: The Hebrew va'etchanan, "I pleaded for grace," gives its name to the Torah portion 3:23–7:11, read in synagogues on the Sabbath after the fast of the Ninth of Av, when the prophetic reading is Isaiah 40, "Comfort, comfort my people." In Hebrew each letter is also a number. The letters of va'etchanan add up to 515, and the midrash (Deuteronomy Rabbah 11:10) says Moses offered 515 prayers to enter the land. The verb comes from chen, "grace": Rashi notes that even Moses did not ask on the basis of his merits but for a free gift.

a: Who is a god in the heavens or on the earth who can do works like yours
p: Moses speaks as if other gods exist. Chapter 4 will say "there is no other." Scholars debate how these fit.
b: The question is like the Song at the Sea: "Who is like you among the gods, O LORD?" (see Exodus 15:11). Read alone, it compares the LORD to other gods as if they existed but were weaker. Yet the same speech ends with "There is no other besides him" (4:35, 39). Many scholars, such as Mark Smith, see a growth in Israel's faith from worship of one God among many to the denial of all others. Others, such as Nathan MacDonald, argue that Deuteronomy's language is about the LORD's unique claim on Israel more than a theory of how many gods exist, so the two kinds of statements do not clash. Traditional readers take "gods" as what the nations call gods.

a: that good hill country, and Lebanon
p: The Sifre and Rashi read "this good hill country" as Jerusalem and "Lebanon" as the temple.
b: Moses longs to see the land he has led Israel toward for forty years. The Sifre reads "this good hill country" as Jerusalem, and "Lebanon" as the temple. The rabbis explain that the temple "makes white" (malbin, from the same letters as levanon) the sins of Israel, and because it was built of Lebanon's cedars. The plain sense is the central hills of Canaan and the mountains of Lebanon to the north, the edges of the promise in 1:7. Whatever the exact meaning, the verse is one of the most human moments in the Torah: the old leader asking simply to see the end of his work.

a: That is enough from you!
p: God says no to Moses, using the same "enough" as in 1:6. Christians have pointed to Moses on the mountain with Jesus.
b: The words rav lakh echo 1:6 and 2:3 (see the note on 1:6). God does not explain again; the refusal stands. Moses is allowed to see the land, not to enter it (3:27; 34:4). Jewish readers have taken it as a lesson on the limits of prayer, even for the greatest prophet. Christian readers since the church fathers have noted that Moses does finally stand in the land in the Gospels, on the mountain where Jesus is transfigured, talking with him and Elijah (Matthew 17:1–3; Luke 9:30–31). Paul, too, asked three times for something and was told no (2 Corinthians 12:8–9).

a: Go up to the top of Pisgah.
p: Pisgah is a ridge at the edge of the Moab plateau, near Mount Nebo, with a wide view west over the Jordan valley.
b: From the heights above the northeast end of the Dead Sea, on a clear day, one can see across to Jericho, the Judean hills and sometimes Jerusalem's Mount of Olives. Deuteronomy 34:1 joins the names: Moses climbs "Mount Nebo, the top of Pisgah." The traditional site, Ras Siyagha on Mount Nebo in Jordan, has had a church in Moses' memory since the 4th century AD. God's order to "lift up your eyes" to the four directions repeats what God told Abraham (Genesis 13:14–15).

a: the valley across from Beth-peor
p: Israel's camp lay near the shrine of Baal of Peor, where the people had just sinned (Numbers 25). Moses was buried there.
b: Beth-peor means "house (temple) of Peor," the place of the god called Baal of Peor. There Israel had joined in Moab's sacrifices and sexual rites, and 24,000 died (Numbers 25:1–9). Moses reminds them of it in 4:3–4. The valley across from Beth-peor is where Moses' speeches were given (4:46) and where God himself buried him, in the valley across from Beth-peor (34:6). The rabbis drew a lesson: Moses' grave was placed opposite Peor to atone for Peor's sin (Bavli Sotah 14a).

a: listen to the rules and the rulings
p: Deuteronomy pairs chuqqim, "rules," with mishpatim, "rulings." This site keeps the same two words throughout the Torah.
b: A choq comes from a verb meaning "to engrave": a fixed rule, written down. A mishpat comes from "to judge": a ruling, a decision of the kind a judge gives. Deuteronomy uses the pair as a name for its whole body of law (4:5, 8, 14; 5:1; 11:32; 12:1). With them come mitzvah, "command," often in the singular for the whole teaching (5:31; 6:1), and edot, "decrees" (4:45). The rabbis tried to tell them apart: Rashi says chuqqim are laws given without a reason, like the food laws, and mishpatim are laws that reason would reach anyway. Most modern scholars think the words overlap. The command to "listen," shema, opens the speeches of 5:1, 6:4 and 9:1 too.

a: Do them so that you may live
p: Obedience brings life. Leviticus 18:5 says the same, and Paul quotes Leviticus in Romans 10:5 and Galatians 3:12.
b: "Live" here means a long, full life in the land (4:40; 5:33), not a reward after death. Leviticus says it this way: "If a human being does them, he will live by them" (Leviticus 18:5). Ezekiel repeats the phrase (Ezekiel 20:11). The rabbis drew from it that one may break most commands to save a life: "live by them, and not die by them" (Bavli Yoma 85b). Paul contrasts "the one who does them will live by them" with the righteousness that comes from faith (Romans 10:5–8; Galatians 3:12), and in Romans 10 he turns to Deuteronomy 30:11–14 for that faith. Jewish and many recent Christian readers stress that in Deuteronomy obedience is a response to grace already given, not a way to earn it.

a: Do not add anything to the word I am commanding you
p: An old formula that guarded treaties and law codes. It returns in 12:32 and at the end of Revelation.
b: Ancient Near Eastern documents protected their wording with the same kind of clause. Hammurabi's laws end with curses on any later king who changes them, and Assyrian treaties warn against altering the oath. Deuteronomy repeats the rule at 12:32, and Proverbs 30:6 applies it to God's words. Revelation 22:18–19 closes with a warning against anyone who adds to or takes away from the words of its prophecy. The rabbis read the verse as a law against adding to a command, such as tying five tassels instead of four (the rule bal tosif). Critics note the irony that Deuteronomy itself revises earlier laws; Bernard Levinson argues it does so while claiming to be the original. Traditional readers answer that the rule binds Israel, not God or his prophets.

a: what the LORD did at Baal-peor
p: The most recent disaster, still fresh in memory: Israel joined Moab's god and many died.
b: Numbers 25:3 says, "Israel tied itself to the Baal of Peor, and the LORD burned with anger against Israel." The verb there, "tied itself," is answered here by its opposite: those who "held on to the LORD" lived (4:4). Moses uses the event as proof from experience: the people listening had seen with their own eyes that idolatry kills and faithfulness gives life. Psalm 106:28–31 and Hosea 9:10 remember Peor as a byword for unfaithfulness. Paul alludes to it in 1 Corinthians 10:8.

a: you who held on to the LORD your God
p: Dabaq means to stick, to cling. It is the word for a man holding to his wife and Ruth holding to Naomi.
b: The verb dabaq is the same verb rendered "sticks close" in Genesis 2:24, of a man and his wife, and "clung" in Ruth 1:14, of Ruth and Naomi. Deuteronomy uses it for Israel's bond with God (10:20; 11:22; 13:4; 30:20). The rabbis asked how a person can cling to God, who is "a devouring fire" (4:24). The Talmud answers: by copying his ways. As he clothes the naked, visits the sick and buries the dead, so should you (Bavli Sotah 14a). Another answer is to cling to the wise and their students (Bavli Ketubot 111b). This site renders the word "hold on to."

a: This will show your wisdom and your understanding to the peoples
p: Israel's laws are meant to impress the nations. Later Jewish writers called the Torah wisdom itself.
b: The law is not a private code but a public witness. When the nations see a people living by just rules, they will praise both the people and their God. Psalm 147:19–20 says of God, "No other nation has he treated like this." Later Jewish wisdom writers made the link complete: Ben Sira says that wisdom is "the book of the covenant of the Most High, the law that Moses commanded" (Sirach 24:23), and the book of Baruch calls wisdom "the book of the commands of God" (Baruch 4:1). Isaiah 2:3 pictures the nations coming to Zion to learn God's teaching.

a: a god as close to it as the LORD our God is to us
p: Other nations had many gods and images. Israel had one God, with no image, who answered when they called.
b: The claim is not that the LORD is small or local, but that he is reachable. "The LORD is near to all who call to him" (Psalm 145:18, a translation made for this note). Deuteronomy 30:14 says the same of his word: it is "very near you." Solomon's prayer at the temple builds on the idea of a God who hears his people's prayers from heaven (1 Kings 8:52). The rabbis contrasted Israel's God with an earthly king who can only be reached through officials: God hears directly (Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 9:1).

a: rules and rulings as just as this whole law
p: The claim invites comparison with other ancient law codes. They share much, and differ in telling ways.
b: Laws from Mesopotamia and Anatolia, such as those of Ur-Nammu, Hammurabi (about 1750 BC) and the Hittites, cover many of the same cases as the Torah: theft, injury, marriage, debts, oxen that gore. Scholars such as Moshe Greenberg have pointed out real differences. In the Torah property crimes do not carry the death penalty, the law protects the foreigner and the slave by name, it sets the weekly Sabbath for everyone, and the whole is given as the word of God to the whole people, not as the decree of a king. Others stress how much is shared. The verse's claim is about righteousness, tsaddiqim: laws that are fair.

a: Do not let them slip from your heart as long as you live.
p: Ramban counted this verse as one of the 613 commands: never forget the day at Sinai.
b: Maimonides did not list this verse in his count of the 613 commands, but Nachmanides (Ramban) added it: a command never to forget the giving of the Torah at Sinai, and to tell it to one's children. In traditional Jewish practice, the daily "six remembrances" said after morning prayer include this verse with others about the exodus, Amalek, the golden calf, Miriam and the Sabbath. The point in Moses' speech is that faith rests on events seen and passed on. The phrase "children and grandchildren" stresses that the memory must cross generations who were not there.

a: with darkness, cloud and deep gloom
p: Moses recalls the scene of Exodus 19–20. Hebrews 12 sets it against the joy of Mount Zion.
b: Exodus describes "thunder and flashes of lightning, a heavy cloud on the mountain," and smoke "like a furnace's smoke" (Exodus 19:16–18; Exodus 20:18–21). Deuteronomy adds that the fire reached "the heart of the sky." Hebrews 12:18–21 recalls this blazing fire, darkness, gloom and storm, and says Christians have come instead to "Mount Zion... the city of the living God." Hebrews draws on the Septuagint of this verse and of 5:22.

a: There was nothing but a voice.
p: Israel heard God but saw no form. The rule against images rests on this. Other texts speak of seeing God.
b: The whole argument of 4:15–24 rests on this verse: since God showed no temunah, "form," at Horeb, no form may be made of him. Yet Exodus 24:10 says the elders "saw the God of Israel," and Numbers 12:8 says Moses "looks at the form of the LORD." Readers reconcile them differently. Many traditional readers say the people saw no form, while a few chosen leaders were given a vision. Maimonides read all such language as describing understanding, not sight. Critical scholars often see two traditions, one of which (Deuteronomy) insists on hearing over seeing. Tryggve Mettinger traces Israel's ban on images of God against the wider practice of the ancient Near East.

a: the Ten Words
p: The Hebrew calls them aseret ha-devarim, "the Ten Words." Jews and Christians divide them in different ways.
b: The Hebrew never calls them "commandments." It says "ten words" (here, 10:4 and Exodus 34:28); the Greek dekalogos, "Decalogue," means the same. The difference matters for how they are counted. In Jewish tradition the first "word" is "I am the LORD your God" (5:6), a statement, not a command. Most Protestants and Orthodox count the ban on other gods and the ban on images as two commands. Catholics and Lutherans, following Augustine, join those two and split the last command on craving into two. All agree there are ten. See the chapter 5 page.

a: two tablets of stone
p: Most art shows five commands on each tablet. Some scholars think each tablet held all ten, as two copies of a treaty.
b: Jewish and Christian art usually shows five commands on each tablet, or (in Christian tradition) duties to God on the first and duties to others on the second. Philo divided them five and five. But ancient treaties were often written in duplicate, one copy for each party, each kept in the temple of that party's god. Meredith Kline argued that the two tablets were two copies of the whole covenant: one for God and one for Israel, both kept in the ark because the ark was both God's shrine and Israel's (10:1–5). The Jerusalem Talmud records the view that each tablet held all ten words (Yerushalmi Shekalim 6:1). Exodus 32:15 says the tablets were written on both sides.

a: whether the likeness of a man or a woman
p: The forbidden images run from humans to animals, birds, creeping things and fish, then sun and stars: Genesis 1 backward.
b: Genesis 1 names the lights, the fish and birds, the land animals and creeping things, and last the human, "male and female" (Genesis 1:14–27). Deuteronomy 4:16–19 lists the same groups in reverse order, using some of the same words (zakhar u-neqevah, "male and female"; remes, "creeping thing"). Scholars such as Michael Fishbane have noticed the echo. The point seems to be that nothing God made may stand in for its Maker. Paul uses the same list when he describes the nations exchanging God's glory for "images resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things" (Romans 1:23).

a: The LORD your God has given them as a share to all the peoples under the whole sky.
t: The stars, given to the nations
p: God allotted the sun, moon and stars to the other nations. The rabbis found this so hard that they said the Greek translators changed it.
b: The verse seems to say that God himself let other nations worship the heavenly bodies, while he kept Israel for himself. Moses' song makes a similar claim about the nations and "the sons of God" (32:8–9, in the Dead Sea Scrolls text). Some readers take it to mean God allowed the nations' error for a time (compare Acts 14:16; 17:30). Others, like Clement of Alexandria, thought the stars were given to the nations as a stepping stone toward the true God. The Talmud lists this verse among the places where the elders who made the Greek translation for King Ptolemy changed the text, adding "to give light to all the peoples" (Bavli Megillah 9b).

a: out of the iron furnace
p: Egypt was a smelting furnace, where Israel was heated and shaped. Kings and Jeremiah repeat the image.
b: An "iron furnace" is a smelting furnace for iron ore, among the hottest fires the ancient world knew. The image presents slavery in Egypt as a time of fierce heat, and perhaps of refining, from which God drew out a people. Solomon uses it in his temple prayer (1 Kings 8:51), and Jeremiah 11:4 quotes it as the setting of the covenant. Isaiah 48:10 speaks of a "furnace of affliction." The rabbis compared Israel to gold refined in fire.

a: to be his own people, his inheritance
p: Nachalah usually means family land. Here Israel is God's own land, as it were.
b: A nachalah was a family's share of land, handed down and not to be sold (Numbers 27:1–11; 1 Kings 21:3). Deuteronomy uses the word both for the land God gives Israel (4:21, 38) and for Israel as God's own share (9:26, 29; 32:9). The double use suggests a likeness: as a family belongs to its land, Israel belongs to God. Paul speaks of God's "inheritance in the saints" in the same spirit (Ephesians 1:18).

a: For the LORD your God is a devouring fire, a jealous God.
p: Hebrews 12:29 quotes these words. "Jealous" means the fierce love of a husband who will not share his wife.
b: Fire is how God appeared at Horeb (4:11–12), and fire is what he becomes to those who betray him. The word qanna', "jealous," is used only of God. In Exodus 34:14 it is his very name: "the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God." The Bible often pictures idolatry as adultery (Hosea 1–3; Jeremiah 3), so God's jealousy is the passion of a betrayed husband, not petty envy. Hebrews 12:29 ends its warning to Christians with this verse: "our God is a devouring fire" (a translation made for this note). The same phrase describes God going ahead of Israel against its enemies (9:3).
orig: אֵשׁ אֹכְלָה הוּא אֵל קַנָּא (esh okhlah hu, el qanna')

a: I call the heavens and the earth as witnesses against you today
p: Ancient treaties called on gods as witnesses. Deuteronomy calls on heaven and earth instead.
b: Hittite and Assyrian treaties close with a list of gods who witness the oath, often ending with "mountains, rivers, springs, the great sea, heaven and earth." Israel's covenant has only one God, who cannot witness against himself in the same way, so heaven and earth themselves are called (30:19; 31:28; 32:1). The prophets take up the image as a courtroom: "Listen, heavens, and give ear, earth" (see Isaiah 1:2). Scholars of all schools see here one of the plainest links between Deuteronomy and treaty forms (see the book's introduction).

a: The LORD will scatter you among the peoples.
p: Verses 25–31 describe exile and return. Readers differ on whether they were written before or after the exile.
b: The traditional reading is that Moses foresaw the exile and the return, centuries in advance; Jewish and Christian readers alike have treated these verses as true prophecy. Many critical scholars think 4:25–31 belongs, with 30:1–10, to a layer added during the Babylonian exile (after 587 BC), when Israel had in fact been scattered and needed hope that God would still receive them. They point to close links with Jeremiah and with Solomon's prayer (1 Kings 8:46–53). Others note that exile was a common threat in ancient treaties and need not be late. The message is the same for every view: even after the worst, God can be found.

a: which cannot see or hear or eat or smell
p: The mockery of idols here grows into whole poems in the Psalms and Isaiah.
b: The punishment fits the sin: a people that wanted images will be left with images, which can do nothing. Psalm 115:4–7 expands the list: idols have mouths but cannot speak, eyes but cannot see, ears but cannot hear, noses but cannot smell. Isaiah 44:9–20 tells of a man who burns half a log to cook his food and carves a god from the rest. The phrase "made by human hands" returns in the New Testament for idols and for temples (Acts 7:48; Acts 17:24–25).

a: and you will find him, when you seek him with all your heart and with all your being
p: Jeremiah's letter to the exiles repeats this promise. Jesus' "seek and you will find" carries the same hope.
b: Jeremiah writes to the exiles in Babylon: "You will seek me and find me, when you search for me with all your heart" (Jeremiah 29:13, a translation made for this note). The phrase "with all your heart and with all your being" appears here for the first time in Deuteronomy and returns in the Shema (6:5), in 10:12, 11:13 and 30:2–10. Jesus' "Keep looking, and you will find" (Matthew 7:7) uses the same pairing of verbs, seeking and finding.

a: in days to come
p: Be'acharit ha-yamim means "in the end of the days." It can mean simply "later on," or the last age.
b: The KJV renders it "in the latter days." The phrase appears in Jacob's blessing (Genesis 49:1), Balaam's oracle (Numbers 24:14), Moses' farewell (31:29) and the prophets (Isaiah 2:2; Hosea 3:5; Daniel 10:14). In most Torah passages it probably means "in the future," without a sense of the end of history. Later Jewish and Christian readers often heard it as the messianic age, and the New Testament speaks of "these last days" as having arrived with Jesus (Hebrews 1:2). Here, the setting is exile and return.

a: For the LORD your God is a God of compassion.
p: The word rachum echoes the LORD's own description of himself in Exodus 34:6.
b: The Hebrew rachum is the first word of God's self-description after the golden calf: "a God compassionate and gracious" (Exodus 34:6). It is related to rechem, "womb," and suggests the love of a mother or father for a child. The promise here is the reverse of 4:26: the God who will scatter is also the God who will not "let you go," the verb used for dropping one's hands from someone. Even exile does not end the covenant with the ancestors.

a: as you have heard it, and lived
p: To hear God's voice and survive was thought impossible. Israel had done it.
b: God told Moses, "no human being can see me and stay alive" (Exodus 33:20), and the people feared that hearing would kill them too (5:24–26). Moses' argument is that no nation has ever had such an experience, and Israel lived to tell it. The verse is part of a sweeping question that runs back to the creation of humanity (4:32): nothing like this has happened since. Christian readers have connected it with the claim that God has now spoken "in a Son" (Hebrews 1:1–2).

a: by a strong hand and an outstretched arm
t: The strong hand and outstretched arm
p: The phrase answers Egyptian royal language. Pharaoh's "strong arm" was a boast of Egypt's kings.
b: Egyptian inscriptions often praise Pharaoh's "strong arm" or describe him with arm raised to strike his enemies, a scene carved on temple walls for two thousand years. James Hoffmeier has argued that the exodus language of God's "strong hand and outstretched arm" deliberately answers that image: the God of Israel, not Pharaoh, is the true king with the mighty arm. Deuteronomy uses the phrase often (5:15; 7:19; 11:2; 26:8). The Passover Haggadah reads 26:8, a verse much like this one, word by word.

a: Apart from him there is no other.
p: The clearest denial of other gods in the Torah. Isaiah 40–48 and a scribe in Mark 12 say the same.
b: This verse and 4:39 say what the first command implied: the LORD alone is God, and there is no other. The language returns in Isaiah: "I am the LORD, and there is no other; besides me there is no God" (Isaiah 45:5, a translation made for this note), and in 1 Kings 8:60. A scribe answers Jesus with it in Mark 12:32. Many critical scholars date this chapter late, near the time of Isaiah 40–55, and see it as Israel's mature monotheism. Traditional readers see it as Moses' own conclusion from what Israel had seen. Some, like Nathan MacDonald, argue that "no other" is a claim about loyalty and power more than a count of beings.

a: Because he loved your ancestors
p: Deuteronomy is the first book to say God chose Israel out of love. Election rests on love, not merit.
b: The verb bachar, "choose," for God's choosing of Israel is new in Deuteronomy (7:6–8; 10:15; 14:2). Its reason is love, and nothing in Israel (7:7; 9:4–6). Jewish thought has always held election to mean a calling and a responsibility. The rabbis said the Torah was offered to all nations and only Israel accepted it (Sifre Deuteronomy 343). Christian theologians debate whether this election is of a nation for service or of individuals for salvation, and Paul works through it in Romans 9–11. Scholars note that "love" in ancient treaties also meant loyalty, so God's love here is both feeling and commitment. The Hebrew then says God chose "his descendants after him," probably meaning Abraham's; the ancient translations made it "their... them" (see the variant).

a: with his own presence
p: The Hebrew says God brought Israel out "with his face," that is, in person.
b: The Hebrew be-fanav, "with his face," means God came in person, not through a messenger. It recalls Exodus 33:14: "My face will go, and I will give you rest." Isaiah 63:9 says, "the angel of his face saved them" (a translation made for this note), and the Passover Haggadah insists that God brought Israel out "not by an angel, not by a seraph, not by a messenger, but the Holy One himself." The Septuagint translated "he himself"; this site keeps the idea of presence.

a: So know today, and take it to heart
p: This verse closes the first paragraph of the Aleinu, a prayer said at the end of every Jewish service.
b: The Aleinu prayer, known from the High Holy Day services of the 3rd century AD and later said daily, praises God as King and ends its first paragraph by quoting this verse. Its second paragraph looks forward to the day when "the LORD will be king over all the earth" (Zechariah 14:9). The phrase "take it to heart," literally "bring it back to your heart," means to think it over until it becomes part of you. The same words return in 30:1.

a: Then Moses set apart three cities on the far side of the Jordan
p: A short story between the speeches. The Talmud says Moses did it because he loved to keep a command, even in part.
b: Numbers 35:14 had ordered six cities of refuge, three on each side of the Jordan. Moses names the three in the east now, though they could not work until the western three were chosen (Joshua 20). The Talmud reads Ecclesiastes 5:10, "The lover of silver never gets his fill of silver," as a picture of Moses: he loved commands and would not let even half of one pass him by (Bavli Makkot 10a). Critical scholars see verses 41–43 as a separate note placed between the first speech and the second. The law of the cities is given in 19:1–13.

a: The cities were Bezer in the wilderness
p: Bezer is named in Mesha's inscription. Ramoth-gilead became a famous fortress. Golan gave its name to a region.
b: King Mesha of Moab says, "I built Bezer, for it was in ruins," on his stone of about 840 BC, which shows the town changed hands between Israel and Moab. Its site is uncertain, perhaps Umm el-Amad near Madaba. Ramoth in Gilead, perhaps Tell er-Rumeith in northern Jordan, was the scene of King Ahab's death (1 Kings 22). Golan in Bashan, perhaps Sahem el-Jolan, gave its name to the Golan Heights. Each city served one of the three eastern tribes.

a: This is the law Moses set before the Israelites.
p: When the Torah scroll is lifted in the synagogue, the people sing this verse.
b: Verses 44–49 are the heading of Moses' second speech, which runs to the end of chapter 28. In the synagogue, after the reading, the open scroll is lifted up for all to see (the hagbahah), and the congregation sings: "This is the Torah that Moses set before the Israelites," adding "at the LORD's word through Moses" from Numbers 9:23. The custom expresses the belief that the scroll in front of them is the same teaching Moses gave.

a: These are the decrees, the rules and the rulings
p: Edot are solemn charges, the terms of a covenant that the people have sworn to. This site calls them "decrees."
b: The word edot comes from the root for "witness" (ed). It can mean a solemn warning given in front of witnesses, and so the binding terms of a covenant. The tablets are called the "tablets of the testimony" (edut) in Exodus 31:18. Related words in Aramaic ('dy) and Akkadian (adê) are the regular names for treaty oaths, as in the loyalty oaths of the Assyrian king Esarhaddon. The KJV has "testimonies," many modern versions "stipulations." This site says "decrees."

a: as far as Mount Sion, that is, Hermon
p: This Sion (Si'on) is another name for Hermon, spelled differently from Zion in Jerusalem.
b: The Hebrew Si'on begins with a different letter from Tsiyyon, Zion, and the two are unrelated. It may mean "the lofty one." The Syriac translation reads "Sirion," as in 3:9, and the NRSV follows it (see the variant). In Greek the two names look alike, which is why some English versions write "Sion" for both.

a: The LORD did not make this covenant with our ancestors.
t: "Not with our ancestors, but with us"
p: Most of the people at Horeb had died. Moses insists the covenant was made with the living, here and now.
b: Strictly, the adults who stood at Horeb had died in the wilderness (2:14–16), and the listeners were children then or not yet born. Moses' words are emphatic: "with us, we, these, here, today, all of us, alive." He is not denying the ancestors' covenant (4:31; 7:12) but making each new generation present at Sinai. The rabbis took it further: the souls of all future Israelites stood at Sinai (see 29:14–15; Bavli Shevuot 39a). The Passover Haggadah says, "In every generation a person must see himself as if he had come out of Egypt." Christian preachers use the same move when they make the gospel's past events present to hearers today.

a: Face to face the LORD spoke with you at the mountain
t: Face to face, yet through Moses?
p: The people heard God directly (5:4), yet Moses stood between them (5:5). Readers have long tried to fit the two together.
b: "Face to face" means directly and personally, as with Moses in Exodus 33:11. But the next verse says Moses stood between God and the people, because they were afraid. Rashi explains that the people heard the Ten Words directly, and Moses stood between them only to pass on the rest. The Talmud records a view that the people heard only the first two words from God and the rest from Moses (Bavli Makkot 24a). Critical scholars often see two traditions joined: one where the people heard God, one where Moses mediated. The verses agree that the Ten were spoken to all, and the rest of the law through Moses (5:22–31).

a: I was standing between the LORD and you
p: Moses as mediator. Paul says the law was given "through angels by the hand of a mediator."
b: The scene here grows into the long speech of 5:23–31, where the people beg Moses to go near for them. Moses' role as go-between is what makes him the model of the true prophet (see 18:15–18). Paul uses the idea in Galatians 3:19–20, where the law was "ordered through angels by a mediator," while God's promise to Abraham came directly. Hebrews 8:6 and 1 Timothy 2:5 call Jesus the mediator of a better covenant. Jewish tradition honors Moses as Moshe Rabbenu, "Moses our teacher," the one through whom the whole Torah came.

a: I am the LORD your God. I brought you out of the land of Egypt, that house of slaves.
p: The Ten Words open with what God has done, not with what Israel must do. See the notes on Exodus 20:2.
b: The wording is the same as in Exodus 20:2. Jewish tradition counts it as the first of the ten words, a statement to believe; Maimonides made it the first of the 613 commands: to know that God exists. Christians usually treat it as a preface. Either way, the order matters. The God who commands is first the God who freed. Deuteronomy builds its whole argument on that order: Israel should keep the law because it was redeemed, not in order to be redeemed (6:20–25; 7:7–8). See the Exodus notes on the counting of the commands and on the word "you," which is singular throughout.

a: an idol in the form of anything
p: Exodus reads "an idol, or the form of anything." Deuteronomy leaves out the "or," which joins the image to the idol.
b: In Exodus 20:4 the Hebrew has "an idol and any form," which can be read as two bans: on carved idols and on any likeness at all. Deuteronomy has "an idol, any form": the "form" describes the idol. The difference is small, but it supports the Jewish and Catholic reading, in which the ban on images belongs with the ban on other gods and forbids images made for worship. Many Protestants, especially in the Reformed tradition, count the ban on images as a separate command and apply it to images of God himself. See the notes on Exodus 20:4.

a: to the third and the fourth generation of those who hate me
p: Does God punish children for their parents? Deuteronomy itself says no court may (24:16). Readers explain the tension.
b: Ancient families lived together in three or four generations, so the phrase may mean the whole household of a man who "hates" God, living at the same time. The Targum and the Talmud add a condition: the children are punished when they hold on to their fathers' deeds (Targum Onkelos; Bavli Berakhot 7a). Deuteronomy 7:10 stresses that God repays the one who hates him "to his face," and 24:16 forbids putting children to death for parents' crimes. Ezekiel 18 later rejects the proverb about sour grapes. See the note on Exodus 20:5.

a: Keep the day of the Sabbath
p: Exodus says "Remember," Deuteronomy "Keep." The rabbis said God spoke both words at once.
b: The fourth word begins with zakhor, "Remember," in Exodus 20:8 and shamor, "Keep" or "Guard," here. The rabbis explained the difference by saying God spoke both words "in one utterance," something no human mouth could do (Mekhilta; Bavli Shevuot 20b). From the pair they drew two sides of the Sabbath: remembering it with blessing, wine and words, and keeping it by not working. The Friday evening hymn Lekha Dodi (16th century) opens with this teaching: "'Keep' and 'Remember' in a single word." Critical scholars see the differences as signs that Deuteronomy's text was revised from an earlier form.

a: as the LORD your God commanded you
p: The fourth and fifth commands add this phrase. It suggests Moses is quoting Words given earlier, at Horeb.
b: Only Deuteronomy's Sabbath and parents commands include "as the LORD your God commanded you" (5:12, 16). The phrase points back to the original giving, as if Moses, forty years later, quotes and explains. Traditional readers take the Exodus wording as the words on the tablets and Deuteronomy's as Moses' retelling with explanation; others say both were spoken. Many critical scholars hold that the Decalogue grew in stages, and that the short commands (5:17–20) are older, while the longer ones received their explanations later in different ways. The chapter 5 page sets out all the differences.

a: Then your slave, man or woman, can rest just as you do.
p: The Hebrew eved can mean a slave, a servant or a royal official. Here it means a slave in an Israelite household.
b: The word eved covers a range: Moses calls himself God's "servant" (3:24), officials are the king's "servants," and here an eved is a worker owned by a household, often for debt (15:12–18). This site renders it by context: "slave" where a person is owned, "servant" where it means service or a title. Deuteronomy's reason for the Sabbath here is new: so that the slaves can rest "just as you do." The next verse grounds it in Israel's own past in Egypt. The Sabbath is a day of equality for the household.

a: Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt
p: Exodus grounds the Sabbath in creation. Deuteronomy grounds it in the exodus. Jews remember both every Friday night.
b: Exodus 20:11 says: "For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth... and on the seventh day he rested." Deuteronomy gives a different reason: God freed Israel from slavery, so Israel must give rest to its own slaves. The two are not in conflict. The Friday evening blessing over wine (Kiddush) names the Sabbath both "a memorial of the work of creation" and "a remembrance of the going out from Egypt." One Dead Sea Scroll, 4QDeut-n, adds the Exodus reason here too (see the variant). "Remember that you were a slave" becomes a refrain in Deuteronomy's laws for the poor (15:15; 16:12; 24:18, 22).

a: and so that it will go well with you
t: "That it may go well with you"
p: Deuteronomy adds this promise. Paul quotes it in Ephesians 6:3, from the Greek.
b: Exodus 20:12 promises only long life on the land. Deuteronomy adds "so that it will go well with you," a phrase it uses often (4:40; 5:29, 33; 6:3, 18). The Septuagint of Exodus also has it, and Paul quotes the longer form in Ephesians 6:2–3, calling this "the first command with a promise." The rabbis compared the honor owed to parents with the honor owed to God (Proverbs 3:9), and said that God, father and mother are three partners in making a person (Bavli Kiddushin 30b–31a).

a: You must not murder.
p: The Hebrew ratsach means unlawful killing. The KJV's "kill" is too broad. See the note on Exodus 20:13.
b: The verb ratsach is used for murder and for killing that brings blood guilt, as in the law of the cities of refuge (4:42; 19:3–6), and almost never for killing in war. In Numbers 35:27 and 35:30, though, it describes the blood avenger's lawful killing and the execution of a murderer, so some scholars prefer "kill unlawfully." Most modern versions say "murder." The KJV's "Thou shalt not kill" has led many readers to apply the command to war or to all killing. Jesus extends it to anger and insults (Matthew 5:21–22), and 1 John 3:15 to hatred.

a: And you must not commit adultery.
p: In Deuteronomy the commands after "You must not murder" are each joined by "and." In Exodus they stand apart.
b: Exodus lists "You must not murder. You must not commit adultery. You must not steal." Deuteronomy says "and you must not" for each command after it (5:18–21). The "and" ties the duties toward one's neighbor into a single chain, as if to say they belong together. James 2:10–11 makes a similar point from a different angle: whoever breaks one command breaks the law as a whole. The Greek order of these commands also differs (see the variant).

a: as an empty witness
p: Exodus says a "lying" witness. Deuteronomy says an "empty" one, the same word as in the command about God's name.
b: Exodus 20:16 has ed shaqer, "a lying witness." Deuteronomy has ed shav', "an empty witness," using the same word shav' that appears in 5:11, "for something empty." An empty witness gives worthless or baseless testimony. Some interpreters think Deuteronomy widens the command from false testimony in court to any worthless claim against a neighbor. The phrase "your neighbor" shows that the setting is the community's court (19:15–21).

a: And you must not crave your neighbor's wife.
p: Deuteronomy lists the wife before the house and gives her a separate verb. This changes how the last command is counted.
b: In Exodus 20:17 the house comes first and the wife is listed with the slaves and animals, all under one verb, chamad, "crave." Deuteronomy puts the wife first, gives her the verb chamad, and uses a second verb, hit'avveh, "long for," for the house and the rest. It also adds "his field," fitting a people about to own land. Many scholars read the change as setting the wife apart from property. Augustine, followed by Catholic and Lutheran tradition, used Deuteronomy's wording to divide this into two commands, the ninth (wife) and the tenth (goods). Whether craving means a feeling or a plan to take is debated; see the note on Exodus 20:17.
orig: לֹא תַחְמֹד... וְלֹא תִתְאַוֶּה (lo tachmod... ve-lo tit'avveh)

a: He added nothing more.
t: "He added no more," or "he did not stop"?
p: The Hebrew lo yasaf can mean God spoke no more words, or that his voice never stopped. The Targum takes the second.
b: The plain sense is that God spoke these Ten Words to all the people and then said nothing more to them directly; the rest came through Moses. The Aramaic Targum Onkelos translates "and he did not stop," and Rashi gives both meanings: the voice was so mighty that it went on and on. The second reading became important in Jewish thought: God's voice from Sinai keeps speaking in every generation's study. Benjamin Sommer has discussed how this verse was read in both ways. Most modern translations follow the first.

a: the voice of the living God
p: The first time the Bible says "the living God." The title runs to David, Peter and Hebrews.
b: The phrase elohim chayyim appears here for the first time. It sets the LORD apart from idols that "cannot see or hear" (4:28). David uses it when he faces Goliath, who insults "the battle lines of the living God" (1 Samuel 17:26). Jeremiah 10:10 calls the LORD "the living God and the everlasting King."
