In the New Testament Peter confesses Jesus as "the Son of the living God" (Matthew 16:16), and Hebrews warns that "it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God" (Hebrews 10:31).
r: Joshua 3:10; 1 Samuel 17:26; Jeremiah 10:10; Psalm 42:2; Matthew 16:16; Hebrews 10:31

a: and we will listen and do it
t: "We will do and we will listen"
p: Exodus 24:7 has "we will do, and we will listen." Here the order is "listen and do." The rabbis made much of the order.
b: At the covenant ceremony in Exodus the people say, "All the LORD has spoken, we will do, and we will listen" (Exodus 24:7). The Talmud praises Israel for promising to do before hearing, and says that angels crowned each Israelite with two crowns for it (Bavli Shabbat 88a). Here the order is the natural one: first hear, then do. Deuteronomy's word shema, "listen," also means "obey," and the book's call is to hear in a way that leads to doing (6:3; 6:4; 30:11–14). James 1:22 says, "Be doers of the word, and not hearers only."

a: Everything they have said is right.
p: The people's fear is approved. Later this scene becomes the basis for the promise of a prophet like Moses.
b: God does not scold the people for asking Moses to go near for them; he approves. This moment is recalled in 18:16–18, where God promises to raise up a prophet like Moses because at Horeb the people asked not to hear God's voice directly again. In the New Testament, Peter and Stephen identify that prophet with Jesus (Acts 3:22–23; Acts 7:37), and the Samaritans, too, awaited such a prophet, the Taheb. The verse shows that God's word can come through a human voice without losing its authority.

a: If only they always had a heart like this
p: The Hebrew mi yitten, "who will give," is a cry of longing. The Talmud says Moses should have answered, "You give it."
b: Literally "Who will give that they have this heart?" It is a wish, and in God's mouth it is striking: God longs for a heart in the people that he does not force. The Talmud says that Israel should have answered, "You give it to us," and that Moses only hinted at this forty years later, when he told them God had not yet given them a heart to know (29:4; Bavli Avodah Zarah 5a–b). The prophets promise the gift: "I will give them a heart to know me" (Jeremiah 24:7; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26), and Deuteronomy 30:6 promises that God will circumcise their hearts.

a: I will tell you the whole command, the rules and the rulings
t: Laws given at Horeb, taught in Moab
p: Moses says the laws of chapters 12–26 were given to him privately at Horeb. They differ in places from the laws of Exodus.
b: The verse explains how Deuteronomy's law relates to Sinai. The people heard the Ten Words; Moses alone heard the rest and now, forty years later, passes it on. Traditional readers hold that the laws of chapters 12–26 were revealed at Horeb with those of Exodus and Leviticus. The rabbis explained differences as two sides of one revelation. Critical scholars point out that many of Deuteronomy's laws revise the Covenant Code of Exodus 21–23 (on slaves, altars and festivals, for example), and suggest that this verse gives the newer laws the authority of Horeb. Bernard Levinson calls this a strategy of "legal innovation" presented as continuity.

a: Do not turn off to the right or to the left.
p: Obedience is a road. Stepping off it to either side is going astray.
b: Deuteronomy pictures obedience as walking a road God has laid out (5:33). The warning not to turn "to the right or to the left" returns for the king (17:20), for the courts (17:11), for the whole people (28:14) and for Joshua (Joshua 1:7). It is the language of Sihon's road too: Moses promised to stay on the highway and not turn aside (2:27). Psalm 1 and Proverbs develop the picture of two ways, and Jesus speaks of the narrow way that leads to life (Matthew 7:13–14).

a: in a land flowing with milk and honey
p: The classic picture of a rich land. The "honey" was probably date or grape syrup as well as bees' honey.
b: The phrase first appears when God speaks to Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:8) and returns about fifteen times in the Torah and about twenty in the whole Old Testament. Milk came mostly from goats and sheep, the wealth of herders. The Hebrew devash means honey, and also the thick syrup made from dates or grapes; the rabbis took the "honey" of 8:8 to be date honey. Beehives have been found at Tel Rehov from the 10th century BC, so bees' honey was also produced. The phrase pictures a land good for both shepherds and farmers.

a: Listen, Israel
p: This verse, called the Shema after its first word, is the center of Jewish prayer, said morning and evening.
b: The Mishnah treats the saying of the Shema, morning and evening, as a duty from these verses (6:7), and the first chapters of tractate Berakhot set its times and rules. The full prayer has three parts: 6:4–9, 11:13–21 and Numbers 15:37–41. Saying it is called "taking on the yoke of the kingdom of heaven" (Mishnah Berakhot 2:2). In Torah scrolls the last letter of the first word (ayin) and of the last word (dalet) are written large; together they spell ed, "witness." Jews have said the Shema at the hour of death, and the Talmud tells that Rabbi Akiva died a martyr's death under Rome with its last word, echad, "one," on his lips (Bavli Berakhot 61b).

a: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one.
t: Four ways to read four words
p: The Hebrew is just "YHWH our God YHWH one." It can be read at least four ways. This site follows one of the most common.
b: The Hebrew has no verb: YHWH eloheinu YHWH echad. Main readings: (1) "The LORD our God, the LORD is one" (many English versions and Jewish prayer books); (2) "The LORD our God is one LORD" (KJV); (3) "The LORD is our God, the LORD alone" (NJPS, and Rashbam and Ibn Ezra in effect); (4) "The LORD is our God; the LORD is one" (this site). Reading (3) stresses loyalty: Israel must worship the LORD alone (compare Zechariah 14:9, where on that day "the LORD will be one"). Reading (1) or (4) stresses God's unity. Rashi joins them: the LORD who is our God now will one day be the one LORD of all nations. Daniel Block argues for "the LORD alone." Jesus quotes the verse in Mark 12:29 in the Greek of the Septuagint, which favors the "one" reading.
orig: יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד (YHWH eloheinu YHWH echad)

a: The LORD is one.
t: One God: Jewish and Christian readings
p: Jews read "one" as God's complete unity. Christians read it as compatible with the Trinity. Paul rewrites it around Jesus.
b: Maimonides made God's unity the second of his thirteen principles: God is one with a oneness unlike any other. Many Jewish thinkers have read the Shema as a direct denial of the Christian Trinity. Some Christian writers argue that echad can describe a compound unity, as in "one flesh" (Genesis 2:24), but most scholars say the word itself does not decide the matter. More significant is that the New Testament keeps the Shema: Jesus calls it the first command (Mark 12:29), and James 2:19 says, "You believe that God is one; you do well." In 1 Corinthians 8:6 Paul splits its words: "one God, the Father... and one Lord, Jesus Christ." Richard Bauckham and N. T. Wright read this as including Jesus within the one God of the Shema.
r: 4:35; Mark 12:28–34; John 10:30; Romans 3:29–30; 1 Corinthians 8:4–6; Galatians 3:20; James 2:19

a: Love the LORD your God
p: In ancient treaties "love" meant loyalty. Deuteronomy asks for that and more: a love of the heart.
b: William Moran showed that "love" in Near Eastern treaties and letters is the language of loyalty: a vassal "loves" his overlord by keeping faith with him, and the Assyrian king Esarhaddon made his subjects swear to "love" his heir "as yourselves." So a command to love makes sense in a covenant. But Deuteronomy also speaks of God's love for Israel as warm and free (7:7–8; 10:15), and it locates Israel's love in the heart. The rabbis asked how one can be commanded to love, and the Sifre answers: by learning God's words, through which one comes to know him. Jesus quoted this verse and said, "This commandment is the great one, and the first" (Matthew 22:37–38).

a: with all your heart, with all your being and with all your strength
p: Lev is the mind and will, nefesh the whole living self, me'od "muchness." The rabbis read the last as "all your money."
b: In Hebrew the lev, "heart," is where a person thinks and decides, not only feels. Nefesh, often "soul," is the whole living person, the self that breathes and desires; this site says "being." Me'od is usually an adverb, "very"; only here and in 2 Kings 23:25 is it a noun: "your very-ness," all you have and are. The Mishnah reads: with both your inclinations, good and evil; with your life, even if he takes it; with all your wealth (Mishnah Berakhot 9:5). The Gospels list four terms, adding "mind" (Mark 12:30), probably because Greek needed two words for the Hebrew lev (see the variant).
orig: בְּכָל־לְבָבְךָ וּבְכָל־נַפְשְׁךָ וּבְכָל־מְאֹדֶךָ (be-khol levavkha u-ve-khol nafshekha u-ve-khol me'odekha)

a: Keep these words I am commanding you today on your heart.
p: The words are to be inside, not only on stone. Jeremiah's new covenant promises the same.
b: The tablets were stone, but the words must also be on the heart. Proverbs speaks this way of wisdom: "Write them on the tablet of your heart" (Proverbs 3:3; Proverbs 7:3). Jeremiah promises a new covenant in which God says, "I will put my law within them and write it on their heart" (Jeremiah 31:33, a translation made for this note), and Paul speaks of a letter "written not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts" (2 Corinthians 3:3). Deuteronomy already moves in this direction: 30:14 says the word is "in your mouth and in your heart."

a: Repeat them to your children again and again.
p: The verb shinnen means to sharpen, as a sword. The Sifre: the words should be sharp in your mouth.
b: The Hebrew ve-shinnantam comes from shanan, "to sharpen" (Psalm 64:3; Proverbs 25:18). Most translators take it as "teach them carefully" or "impress them," or connect it with shanah, "to repeat." The Sifre reads: let the words be so sharp in your mouth that if someone asks you, you answer at once without stammering. The rabbis also counted pupils as "children," so the command covers teaching anyone. This verse is the basis for Jewish schooling of children, and Josephus boasts that Jewish children learned the laws "from our first awareness" (Against Apion 2.178).

a: when you go to bed and when you get up
p: The rabbis drew from these words the duty to say the Shema twice a day, at bedtime and on rising.
b: The Mishnah opens with the question: "From what time may the Shema be said in the evening?" (Mishnah Berakhot 1:1). Hillel's school read this verse as giving the times: when people lie down and when they get up. Shammai's school read it as giving the posture: lying down at night and standing in the morning. Hillel's view became the rule. The pairs in the verse, sitting and walking, lying down and rising, are a way of saying "all the time and everywhere."

a: Tie them as a sign on your hand, and let them be a band between your eyes.
p: Jews wear tefillin from this verse. Some read it as a figure of speech. Tefillin from Qumran show the custom is ancient.
b: Rabbinic Judaism reads the verse literally: men tie small leather boxes, tefillin, holding this passage and three others (11:13–21; Exodus 13:1–16), on the arm and forehead during weekday morning prayer. The Greek word "phylacteries" appears in Matthew 23:5, and many tefillin cases and slips were found at Qumran; Yigael Yadin published a set from the 1st century BC that includes the Ten Words. The Karaites, and the medieval commentator Rashbam on Exodus 13:9, took the language as a figure, like Proverbs 3:3, "Tie them around your neck." Most scholars think the verse began as a metaphor and became a practice, or that both existed early. The Letter of Aristeas and Josephus (Antiquities 4.213) already know the custom.
orig: וּקְשַׁרְתָּם לְאוֹת עַל־יָדֶךָ וְהָיוּ לְטֹטָפֹת בֵּין עֵינֶיךָ (u-qeshartam le-ot al-yadekha ve-hayu le-totafot ben enekha)

a: Write them on the doorposts of your house and on your city gates.
p: Jewish homes carry a small case on the doorpost, holding this passage and 11:13–21. The word mezuzah means "doorpost."
b: The Hebrew word for doorpost, mezuzah, became the name of the small scroll with 6:4–9 and 11:13–21 fixed to the right doorpost of Jewish homes, often in a decorative case. Mezuzah scrolls were found at Qumran too. In the ancient Near East, protective words and signs were often put on doorways, and Egyptian homes sometimes had sayings on door frames; Exodus 12:7 has the Passover blood on the doorposts. Samaritans carved the Ten Words on stones set at their doors. Maimonides insisted the mezuzah is a reminder of God's unity and love, not a charm to guard the house.

a: It has large, fine cities that you did not build
p: Israel receives towns, houses, wells and vineyards it did not make. Joshua 24:13 repeats the list. The danger is forgetting.
b: The list is deliberately long: cities you did not build, houses you did not fill, wells you did not dig, vines and olives you did not plant. At the end of the conquest, Joshua repeats God's words: "I gave you a land you had not worked on, and towns you had not built" (Joshua 24:13). Nehemiah 9:25 recalls the same gifts. Moses' warning, here and in 8:11–18, is that gifts can make people forget the giver. Jesus says something similar to his followers: "Others toiled, and you have come in on their toil" (John 4:38).

a: It is the LORD your God you must fear.
p: Jesus quotes this verse when Satan offers him the kingdoms of the world. Matthew's "only" comes from the Greek.
b: In the third temptation Jesus answers, "Worship the Lord your God, and serve him only" (Matthew 4:10; Luke 4:8). The Hebrew puts the object first for emphasis, "the LORD your God you must fear, him you must serve." Some Septuagint manuscripts read "worship" and add "only," the form the Gospels quote. All three of Jesus' answers in the desert come from these chapters of Deuteronomy (8:3; 6:16; 6:13), where Israel was tested in the wilderness for forty years. Christians read Jesus' forty days as the faithful Son passing the test where Israel had failed. The command to "swear by his name" was a sign of loyalty; Jesus later urged his followers not to swear at all (Matthew 5:33–37).

a: the way you tested him at Massah
p: At Massah the people demanded water as proof that God was with them. Jesus refused to test God this way.
b: Massah means "Testing." Exodus 17:7 tells how the people "put the LORD on trial, saying, 'Is the LORD here with us, or isn't he?'" To test God is to demand that he prove himself on our terms, as a condition of trust. In the second temptation Satan quotes Psalm 91 and asks Jesus to throw himself from the temple; Jesus answers with this verse (Matthew 4:7). Psalm 95:8–9 and Hebrews 3:8–9 also recall Massah. Judith, a book Catholic and Orthodox Christians include in the Old Testament, turns the verse on a town that gave God five days to save it (Judith 7:30). Judith asks its rulers, "Now who are you, to put God to the test today, and to stand in God's place among human beings?" (Judith 8:12). The rabbis, by contrast, noted one place where God invites testing: the tithe (Malachi 3:10).
r: 9:22; 33:8; Exodus 17:1–7; Psalm 95:8–9; Malachi 3:10; Matthew 4:5–7; Hebrews 3:8–9; Judith 7:30; Judith 8:12

a: Do what is right and good in the LORD's eyes.
t: Beyond the letter of the law
p: Ramban read this verse as a command to do good even where no law speaks: going beyond what the rules require.
b: Nachmanides (Ramban) explains that the Torah cannot list every case of human dealings, so after its specific laws it gives a general command: do what is right and good. From this the rabbis drew practices such as a neighbor's right to buy adjoining land first, and the ideal of acting "within the line of the law" (lifnim mi-shurat ha-din), giving up one's strict rights for the sake of fairness (Bavli Bava Metzia 108a; 30b). The verse is a reminder that Deuteronomy's laws aim at a way of life, not only at rules to obey.

a: What do they mean, the decrees, the rules and the rulings the LORD our God commanded you?
p: The Passover Haggadah puts this question in the mouth of the "wise son," one of four children at the Seder.
b: The Haggadah describes four children: the wise, the wicked, the simple and the one who does not know how to ask. The wise child asks this verse's question; the wicked child asks, "What is this service to you?" (Exodus 12:26), and is rebuked for saying "to you" and so excluding himself. But the wise child also says "you." The Septuagint and the Jerusalem Talmud's version of the Haggadah read "us" here (see the variant), which may be the older form of the Seder text. The answer in 6:21–25 is a short creed of the exodus.

a: We were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt
p: These words begin the answer at the heart of the Passover Seder: "We were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt."
b: The Haggadah takes this verse as the opening of its main answer to the child's questions: "We were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt, and the LORD our God brought us out from there with a strong hand." The father speaks of himself as one of the slaves. The verse is one of the short summaries of Israel's faith in Deuteronomy, with 26:5–9, that Gerhard von Rad called "little creeds." The law, in this answer, is the shape of life for a people set free.

a: And it will be our righteousness
p: Keeping the law is called "righteousness." Jews and Christians, and Christians among themselves, read this differently.
b: The Hebrew tsedaqah means being in the right, doing what a relationship requires. Here it is the standing of a people who keep the covenant before God. Jewish readers take it plainly: faithful obedience is righteousness, within a covenant God gave by grace. Paul contrasts "the righteousness that is from the law" with "the righteousness that is from faith" (Romans 10:5–6; Philippians 3:9), and Reformation readers saw this verse as the law's demand, which no one fully meets. Many scholars since E. P. Sanders argue that ancient Judaism never saw obedience as earning God's favor, and that Deuteronomy itself puts grace first (6:21–23). Genesis 15:6 uses the same word for Abram's trust: "he reckoned it to him as righteousness."

a: the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites
p: The list of Canaan's peoples usually has six names. Here there are seven, a number of completeness.
b: Lists of the peoples of Canaan appear about two dozen times in the Bible, with three to twelve names; Exodus 3:8 has six. Deuteronomy's seven may be meant as a full count. Some names are well known: the Canaanites and Amorites appear in Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts, and the Jebusites held Jerusalem until David (2 Samuel 5:6–9). "Hittites" probably means groups in Canaan linked by name to the Hittite empire of Anatolia or its successors in Syria. The Girgashites, Perizzites and Hivites are little known outside the Bible. Many scholars see the list as more a traditional formula than a census.
r: 20:17; Genesis 15:19–21; Exodus 3:8; Exodus 23:23; Joshua 3:10; Joshua 24:11; Acts 13:19

a: you must put them under the ban completely
t: Ban them, and do not marry them?
p: If every Canaanite was to die, why forbid marriage with them? The command seems aimed at their religion as much as their lives.
b: The verse commands the ban (see 2:34), and the next verses forbid covenants and marriage. If the ban were carried out fully, the second rule would not be needed. Many scholars conclude that in Deuteronomy the ban is mainly a way of insisting on total separation from Canaanite worship: the reason given is "they will turn your sons away" (7:4), and the actions commanded are against altars and idols (7:5). Joshua and Judges show many Canaanites still living in the land (Joshua 16:10; Judges 1:27–36), and Rahab and the Gibeonites joined Israel. Traditional Jewish law (Maimonides) held that even the seven nations were first offered peace. The ethical questions are serious and are taken up on the topic page.

a: Do not marry into their families.
p: The ban is on marriage with the seven nations, for religious reasons. Later, Ezra applied it to other peoples too.
b: The verb chatan means to become related by marriage. The reason given is religious, not racial: they will lead your children to other gods (7:4). Solomon's foreign wives proved the point (1 Kings 11:1–8). After the exile Ezra and Nehemiah extended the rule to Moabites, Ammonites, Egyptians and others (Ezra 9:1–2; Nehemiah 13:23–27). Yet Ruth the Moabite married Boaz and became David's ancestor, and Moses himself had married a Midianite. Rabbinic law understood the rule to forbid marriage with those who had not joined Israel's faith; a foreigner who converted could marry an Israelite. Paul's "do not be yoked with unbelievers" (2 Corinthians 6:14) has often been read in the same spirit.
r: 7:4; 23:3–8; Exodus 34:15–16; 1 Kings 11:1–8; Ezra 9:1–2; Nehemiah 13:23–27; Ruth 4:13–17; 2 Corinthians 6:14

a: chop down their Asherah poles
p: Asherah was a Canaanite goddess, and her symbol was a wooden pole or tree. Inscriptions mention "YHWH and his Asherah."
b: Texts from Ugarit name Athirat (Asherah) as the mother goddess and wife of the high god El. In the Bible, an asherah is usually a wooden object set up near an altar, a pole or stylized tree, and sometimes the goddess herself (1 Kings 18:19; 2 Kings 23:4). Inscriptions from Kuntillet Ajrud in Sinai and from Khirbet el-Qom, from about 800 BC, bless people "by YHWH... and his Asherah." Scholars such as William Dever take this as evidence that many Israelites worshiped the goddess beside the LORD; others read "his asherah" as the wooden symbol at his shrine. The "standing stones" (matsevot) were upright stones marking holy places. Genesis tells of patriarchs setting them up, but Deuteronomy forbids them (16:22).

a: his own private treasure
p: The Hebrew segullah is a king's personal treasure, as in Exodus 19:5. Peter applies it to the church.
b: A segullah was property set aside for oneself, like a king's private treasury (1 Chronicles 29:3; Ecclesiastes 2:8). The related Akkadian word sikiltu means personal property set aside, as Moshe Greenberg showed, and a seal impression from Alalakh in Syria calls its owner "the servant of Adad, the beloved of Adad, the sikiltum of Adad." At Ugarit a Hittite king reminds the king of Ugarit that he is his servant, his sglt, the closest parallel to the covenant use. Exodus 19:5–6 first gives Israel this title along with "a kingdom of priests, a holy nation." Deuteronomy repeats it (14:2; 26:18), and Malachi 3:17 uses it again. Peter applies the language to Christians: "a people for God's own possession" (1 Peter 2:9). Being "holy" here is a status given, not first a moral achievement: Israel is set apart because God chose it.

a: You were the fewest of all the peoples.
p: Israel is called the smallest of nations, even though 1:10 says they are like the stars. Both are true in different ways.
b: The verse seems to clash with 1:10 and 10:22, and with the 603,550 fighting men of Numbers 1:46. Many readers say Israel was small compared to the great nations around it, and that the comparison is with the "seven nations bigger and stronger than you" (7:1). Others see it as support for the view that Israel's real numbers in the wilderness were much smaller (see the census topic). The point of the verse, however, is theological: God did not choose Israel for its size. The rabbis read it as praise: Israel made itself small before God, unlike Pharaoh or Nebuchadnezzar who made themselves great (Bavli Chullin 89a).

a: It was because the LORD loved you
p: Why did God choose Israel? Because he loved them. The text gives no further reason, and that is the point.
b: Verses 7–8 rule out a reason in Israel: not numbers, and later not righteousness (9:4–6). What is left is God's love and his oath to the ancestors. The logic seems circular, "he loved you because he loved you," and many readers think that is deliberate: love that is chosen cannot be explained by something outside itself. The New Testament uses the same pattern: "In this is love, not that we loved God but that he loved us" (1 John 4:10), and "God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). Theologians call this the "scandal of particularity"; Jon Levenson explores it as the love of a father for a chosen son.

a: ransomed you from the house of slaves
p: The verb padah means to ransom, to buy back. Deuteronomy uses it for the exodus.
b: Padah is the word for buying back a firstborn son or a slave (Exodus 13:13; Exodus 21:8). Deuteronomy uses it for what God did in Egypt (9:26; 13:5; 15:15; 21:8; 24:18): he bought Israel out of slavery. The Septuagint used lytroō, "to ransom," the word family behind Jesus' saying that he came "to give his life as a ransom in place of many" (Mark 10:45). In Deuteronomy there is no price paid to Pharaoh; the stress is on God's power, "with a strong hand." See also the related word go'el, "redeemer."

a: for a thousand generations
p: This verse explains the "thousands" of the Ten Words: God's loyal love lasts for a thousand generations.
b: The Ten Words say God shows loyal love "to thousands" (5:10; Exodus 20:6). This verse makes clear that it means a thousand generations, set against the "third and fourth generation" of punishment. Psalm 105:8 says God remembers his covenant "for a thousand generations." The rabbis noted that the measure of God's goodness is many times greater than the measure of his punishment (Tosefta Sotah 4:1). The word hesed is the covenant loyalty that keeps going; this site always renders it "loyal love."

a: But he pays back to their face those who hate him, by destroying them.
p: "To their face" may mean in person, or in their own lifetime. The Targum reads it as a reward now and judgment later.
b: The verse seems to correct a possible misreading of 5:9: the one who hates God is himself repaid, not only his children. "To his face" probably means personally and directly. Targum Onkelos reads it as "in his lifetime": God pays the wicked the good they have done in this life, so as to destroy them in the world to come. Rashi follows this. Christian readers often connect the delay of judgment with God's patience (Romans 2:4–6; 2 Peter 3:9). The verse also insists, against appearances, that God "will not be slow."

a: If you listen to these rulings
p: The verse opens with eqev, "as a result of," literally "heel." It names a weekly Torah portion. Rashi drew a lesson from the word.
b: The Hebrew eqev means "because of, as a result of," and comes from the word for "heel." The weekly Torah reading 7:12–11:25 is called Ekev after it. Rashi, following a midrash, reads it as a hint: if you keep even the "light" commands that people trample with their heels, God will keep his covenant with you. Mishnah Avot 2:1 makes the same point: be as careful with a light command as with a weighty one, since you do not know the reward of each.

a: the calves of your herds and the lambs of your flocks
t: Names of gods as farm words
p: The Hebrew words for "calves" and "lambs" here are the names of the Canaanite gods Sheger and Ashtart.
b: The phrase shegar alafekha ve-ashterot tsonekha uses two rare words. Sheger is known from Ugarit and from the Balaam inscription of Deir Alla as the name of a god of animal fertility, and ashterot is the plural of Ashtart (Astarte), the goddess of fertility. In Hebrew they have become ordinary words for the young of cattle and sheep. Scholars see a quiet polemic: what the Canaanites thanked their gods for, Israel receives from the LORD, and the gods' names are reduced to farm words. The triad "grain, new wine and olive oil" likewise names the land's three main crops, sometimes linked with gods elsewhere.
orig: שְׁגַר־אֲלָפֶיךָ וְעַשְׁתְּרֹת צֹאנֶךָ (shegar alafekha ve-ashterot tsonekha)

a: any of the evil diseases of Egypt that you know about
p: God promised at Marah that the sickness he laid on Egypt would not come on Israel. Deuteronomy repeats the promise and its reverse.
b: At Marah God said, "None of the sickness I laid on Egypt will I lay on you. For I am the LORD, your healer" (Exodus 15:26). "The diseases of Egypt" may mean the plagues, or the illnesses for which Egypt was known in the ancient world; Egyptian medical texts describe many of them. Deuteronomy 28:27 and 28:60 turn the promise around: if Israel breaks the covenant, the diseases of Egypt will cling to it. The promise of health is part of the blessings of covenant faithfulness (7:12–16).

a: The LORD your God will even send the hornet among them
p: Literal insects, panic, or Egypt? Readers have offered all three.
b: The tsir'ah appears also in Exodus 23:28 and Joshua 24:12: "I sent the hornet out in front of you, and it drove them from your path." (1) Some read it literally: swarms of hornets drove people from their hiding places, as the verse says. (2) Many modern commentators read it as a picture of panic and terror (compare 7:23). (3) John Garstang suggested that it stands for Egypt, since the bee was a symbol of the pharaoh of Lower Egypt, and Egyptian campaigns had weakened Canaan before Israel arrived. The Talmud says the hornet shot poison at the Canaanites' eyes (Bavli Sotah 36a). The context favors God's hidden help in many forms.

a: bit by bit
p: The conquest would be slow. Exodus gives a practical reason; Judges gives a spiritual one.
b: Exodus 23:29–30 says: "I will not drive them all out in one year, so that the land does not become a waste and the wild animals grow too many for you. Bit by bit I will drive them out." Deuteronomy repeats the practical reason. Judges gives two others: Israel's own disobedience (Judges 2:1–3, 20–21), and God's choice to leave nations "to test Israel" and to teach war to a generation that had not known it (Judges 2:22–3:4). Archaeology too suggests that Israel's settlement of the hill country happened gradually over a long period.

a: For it is abhorrent to the LORD your God.
p: To'evah is something utterly repugnant to God or to people. This site renders it "abhorrent."
b: The word to'evah is a favorite of Deuteronomy, used for idols and their trappings (7:25–26; 12:31; 13:14), for unclean food (14:3), for blemished sacrifices (17:1), for cross-dressing (22:5), for crooked weights (25:16) and for other acts. Leviticus uses it for certain sexual acts (Leviticus 18:22–30). Older translations have "abomination," newer ones "detestable." Proverbs speaks of what is a to'evah to the LORD, such as lying lips and false scales (Proverbs 11:1; Proverbs 12:22). The silver and gold on an idol are abhorrent not in themselves but because of what they serve.

a: or you will be put under the ban as it is
p: Taking banned goods makes the taker banned. Joshua 7 tells the story of Achan, who did just that.
b: Whatever is under the ban is "infected" with it: anyone who takes it becomes cherem too. At Jericho, Achan hid silver, gold and a fine robe from the banned city; Israel was defeated at Ai, and Achan and his household were killed (Joshua 7:1–26). 13:15–17 applies the same rule to an Israelite town that turns to other gods. The rule explains why "do not crave" (7:25) is so serious here: it uses the same verb chamad as the tenth word (5:21), and Achan confesses, "I craved them and took them" (Joshua 7:21, a translation made for this note). 2 Maccabees, which Catholic and Orthodox churches hold as Scripture but Protestants and Jews do not, applies the same law when Judas's men find "objects consecrated to the idols of Jamnia" under the tunics of their dead and take them as the reason those men fell (2 Maccabees 12:40).

a: to humble you and to test you, to know what was in your heart
t: Why would God need to test?
p: If God knows everything, why test Israel "to know" its heart? Jewish and Christian thinkers have offered several answers.
b: The wilderness is a school (8:2–5). The verb nissah, "to test," is used of God testing Abraham (Genesis 22:1) and Israel with the manna (Exodus 16:4). Readers ask how God can test "to know." Ramban says a test is for the one tested: it turns a person's potential into action, so that he is rewarded for real deeds. Maimonides says tests make known to others what a person is like (Guide of the Perplexed 3:24). Others read "to know" as "to make known," or as the Bible's way of speaking in human terms. James 1:2–4 and 1 Peter 1:6–7 speak of trials as refining faith.
r: 8:16; 13:3; Genesis 22:1; Exodus 16:4; Exodus 20:20; Judges 2:22; James 1:2–4; 1 Peter 1:6–7

a: He did it to teach you that people do not live by bread alone.
p: Jesus answers the devil's first temptation with this verse. The manna taught that life depends on God's word.
b: When the devil tells the hungry Jesus to turn stones into bread, he answers: "A person will not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes out of the mouth of God" (Matthew 4:4; Luke 4:4, a translation made for this note). In Deuteronomy the lesson came through hunger and manna. The point is not that bodily food does not matter, but that God's word, his command and promise, is what gives life, even in the form of food no one had known. Many readers see the verse as the key to the manna story: bread "from heaven" was itself God's word made food. Jesus' words "Doing what the one who sent me wants, and bringing his work to completion: that is my food" (John 4:34) and his saying that he is "the bread of life" (John 6:35) build on the same idea.
r: 8:16; Exodus 16:4; Exodus 16:15; Matthew 4:1–4; Luke 4:1–4; John 4:34; John 6:31–35

a: People live by everything that comes out of the LORD's mouth.
p: The Hebrew has "everything that comes from the LORD's mouth." The Greek added "word," and the Gospels follow it.
b: The Hebrew kol motsa' fi YHWH means "all that goes out of the LORD's mouth," without the word "word." Some take it to mean whatever God decrees, including food like manna: people live not only by ordinary bread but by anything God commands to nourish them (so Rashbam and Ibn Ezra). Others take it to mean God's spoken word, his commands and promises, which is how the Septuagint and the Gospels read it ("every word," panti rhēmati). The KJV's "every word" follows the Greek. Both readings fit the context; see the variant.

a: Your clothes did not wear out on you
t: Clothes that did not wear out
p: The rabbis imagined clothes that grew with the children and were kept clean by the clouds of glory.
b: Deuteronomy repeats the claim in 29:5, and Nehemiah 9:21 recalls it. The midrash, followed by Rashi, says the clouds of glory washed and pressed the people's clothes, and that children's clothes grew with them like a snail's shell. Modern readers often take the verse as poetic: God's care was so complete that the people lacked nothing they needed. Either way, the verse is a reminder that the wilderness years, remembered as punishment, were also years of provision.

a: the LORD your God trains you the way a man trains his son
p: God's hard lessons are the discipline of a father. Proverbs and Hebrews repeat the idea.
b: The verb yasar means to train, correct or discipline, the work of a parent with a child (21:18). "The LORD disciplines the one he loves, as a father the son he delights in" (Proverbs 3:12, a translation made for this note). Hebrews 12:5–11 quotes Proverbs and applies it to the hardships of Christians: "God is treating you as sons." The verse continues the picture of 1:31, where God carries Israel like a son, and of Exodus 4:22, "Israel is my son, my firstborn."

a: a land of wheat and barley, of vines, figs and pomegranates, a land of olive oil and honey
p: The rabbis called these the seven foods of the land. Only these were brought as first fruits to the temple.
b: The Mishnah rules that first fruits (26:1–11) were brought only from these seven: wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives and dates, since "honey" was taken to mean date honey (Mishnah Bikkurim 1:3). The verse also shapes Jewish blessings: after eating food from the seven species, a special blessing is said, and they come first among foods to be blessed (Bavli Berakhot 41a). The list moves from field crops to orchard trees, and pictures a land where farmers can live well. They are still symbols of the land of Israel on coins and in art.

a: Its stones are iron, and you can dig copper out of its hills
p: Copper was mined in the Arabah south of the Dead Sea from early times. Iron was found in Gilead and elsewhere.
b: Ancient copper mines and smelting sites have been excavated at Timna and at Faynan (biblical Punon, Numbers 33:42) in the Arabah, with major production in the 11th–9th centuries BC. Iron ore occurs in the hills of Gilead, at Mugharat el-Wardeh in the Ajlun hills of Jordan, and in Lebanon. The Hebrew says copper, nechoshet, which older English Bibles call "brass." Job 28:1–2 describes miners digging copper and iron from stone. The verse pictures a land rich in what lies under the ground, as well as on it.

a: When you have eaten and are full, bless the LORD your God for the good land he has given you.
p: This verse is the source of the Jewish grace after meals, the only blessing at a meal the rabbis counted as a Torah command.
b: The Talmud reads this verse as a command to say grace after eating a meal of bread, the Birkat ha-Mazon (Bavli Berakhot 21a, 48b). Its traditional blessings follow the verse: one for food ("When you have eaten and are full"), one for the land ("the good land"), and one for Jerusalem, with a fourth added later. The rabbis drew a further lesson: if one blesses God after eating, all the more before. Christians took over the habit of thanksgiving at meals (1 Timothy 4:4–5).

a: with its burning snakes and scorpions
p: The "burning" or seraph snakes of the wilderness recall Numbers 21 and the bronze snake.
b: The Hebrew nachash saraf, "burning snake," probably refers to the burning pain of the bite, or to a fiery color. Numbers 21:6 says, "So the LORD sent the burning snakes among the people," and tells how Moses made a bronze snake on a pole. Isaiah speaks of flying seraph snakes in the desert of the Negev (Isaiah 30:6). The Sinai and Negev are still home to vipers and scorpions. The description shows how hostile the wilderness was, and so how great God's care.

a: He brought water out of the flint rock for you.
p: Water from the hardest rock. Paul says the rock was Christ.
b: The stories are told in Exodus 17:1–7, at Massah and Meribah near Horeb, where God said, "You will hit the rock, and water will flow out of it," and in Numbers 20:2–13 at Kadesh. "Flint" stresses the miracle: it is the least likely stone to give water. Psalm 114:8 sings of the God who "turned the flint into a spring of water" (a translation made for this note). Jewish legend spoke of a well that followed Israel through the wilderness, and Paul writes, "they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4).

a: My own strength and the power of my hand have won me this wealth.
p: The danger of plenty is pride. The prophets and Jesus warn against the same boast.
b: Moses expects success to be more dangerous than hunger: in the desert Israel had to trust; in the land it might forget (8:11–14). Hosea 13:6 describes exactly this: "When they had grazed, they were full... their heart was lifted up; so they forgot me" (a translation made for this note). Jesus tells the story of a rich man who says to himself that he has plenty laid up for many years, and God calls him a fool (Luke 12:16–21). Paul asks, "What do you have that you did not receive?" (1 Corinthians 4:7). Wealth itself is not condemned here: God gives "the strength to win wealth" (8:18).

a: He is the one who gives you the strength to win wealth
p: Chayil means both strength and wealth. The Targum reads it as "the wisdom to gain property."
b: The Hebrew la'asot chayil, "to make strength," is used for gaining wealth (as in 8:17), and the same word chayil describes an army, a capable person, or riches. Targum Onkelos paraphrases "he gives you counsel to acquire property," and the rabbis drew from the verse that a person's skill in business is God's gift. The purpose clause is striking: God gives wealth "in order to keep his covenant," that is, to fulfill his promises to the ancestors.

a: the one crossing over ahead of you, a devouring fire
p: The "devouring fire" of 4:24, a warning to Israel, now goes ahead of Israel against its enemies.
b: In 4:24 the LORD is "a devouring fire" toward an unfaithful Israel. Here the same God crosses the Jordan first and burns a path. Moses answers the people's old fear of the Anakim (1:28; 9:2) not by denying their size but by pointing to the one who goes ahead. Joshua 3:11 has the ark of "the Lord of all the earth" cross before the people. The two uses of the image belong together: God's fire protects the faithful and threatens the faithless.

a: do not say to yourself, 'The LORD brought me in to take possession of this land because I am righteous.'
p: Three times Moses denies that Israel earned the land. Paul borrows the opening words in Romans 10:6.
b: Verses 4–6 say it three ways: not because of your righteousness, not because of your upright heart, not because you are righteous. The land is a gift, and the people who receive it are "stiff-necked" (9:6). Literally the verse begins "Do not say in your heart." Paul opens his reading of 30:12–14 in Romans 10:6 with the same words in Greek, "Do not say in your heart," and many scholars think he borrowed them from this verse on purpose: the righteousness that comes by faith does not boast of its own goodness. Jewish teachers drew a similar lesson against pride in one's merits.

a: It is because these nations are wicked
t: Why the nations lost their land
p: The conquest is presented as judgment on the nations' evil, not reward for Israel's goodness.
b: Genesis 15:16 had said that Abraham's descendants would return only "in the fourth generation... for the guilt of the Amorites is not yet full." In Leviticus 18:24–28 the land "vomited out" its people for their sexual crimes, and Deuteronomy names child sacrifice and sorcery (12:31; 18:9–12). Defenders of the account point out that the same land would expel Israel for the same sins (4:26–27; 28:63). Critics answer that the charge against the Canaanites comes from their conquerors, and that archaeology shows Israelites and Canaanites had much in common. Both sides agree that the text means to deny Israel any moral superiority.

a: You are a stiff-necked people.
p: The picture is an ox that will not bend its neck to the yoke. God used the phrase of Israel at the golden calf.
b: An ox that stiffens its neck refuses to be yoked and guided. God says of Israel at Sinai, "Look, they are a stiff-necked people" (Exodus 32:9), and Moses repeats it in his prayer (Exodus 34:9). 10:16 calls on Israel to stop hardening its neck, and 31:27 uses the phrase in Moses' last warning. Jeremiah 7:26 and 2 Chronicles 36:13 repeat it, and Stephen hurls it at his judges: "Stiff-necked men, uncircumcised in your hearts and in your ears! You are always fighting the Holy Spirit" (Acts 7:51).

a: you have kept on rebelling against the LORD
p: Moses' own nation is the subject of his harshest review. Psalms 78 and 106 and Stephen's speech follow the same pattern.
b: Moses' second retelling of the wilderness (9:7–10:11) is not a story of heroes but of rebels, "from the day you came out of the land of Egypt" (9:7) to "from the day I first knew you" (9:24). Few national histories are so self-critical. Psalm 78 and Psalm 106 tell Israel's past the same way, and Ezekiel 20 goes further. Stephen's speech in Acts 7 follows the pattern and ends with an accusation. Jewish tradition reads chapter 9 as a model of honest memory: the people must remember their failures in order not to repeat them.

a: Bread I did not eat, and water I did not drink.
t: Forty days, twice or three times
p: Moses fasted forty days on the mountain, and again forty days in prayer. The rabbis counted three periods and dated Yom Kippur from them.
b: Exodus mentions a fast of forty days and nights only in 34:28. Deuteronomy has two: one while receiving the first tablets (9:9) and one in prayer after the calf (9:18, 25; 10:10). The rabbinic chronology Seder Olam, followed by Rashi, counts three periods of forty days: from Sivan 7 to Tammuz 17, when the tablets were broken; forty days of prayer; and forty more from Elul 1 until the second tablets were given on the 10th of Tishri, which became the Day of Atonement. Elijah later walked forty days and nights to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8), and Jesus fasted forty days in the wilderness before being tested (Matthew 4:2).

a: written by the finger of God
p: The tablets were God's own handwriting. Jesus uses "the finger of God" for his power over demons.
b: Exodus 31:18 calls them "stone tablets written by God's own finger." Egypt's magicians confessed, "It is the finger of God" (Exodus 8:19), when they could not copy the gnats. Psalm 8:3 calls the heavens "the work of your fingers." In Luke 11:20 Jesus says, "If I cast out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you." Some church fathers, such as Augustine, linked the finger of God with the Holy Spirit (compare Matthew 12:28) and drew a parallel between the law given at Sinai and the Spirit given at Pentecost.
r: 10:4; Exodus 8:19; Exodus 31:18; Exodus 32:16; Psalm 8:3; Luke 11:20; 2 Corinthians 3:3

a: on the day of the assembly
p: The Hebrew qahal, "assembly," was translated ekklesia in Greek, the word the New Testament uses for "church."
b: Deuteronomy calls the day at Horeb "the day of the assembly" (9:10; 10:4; 18:16). The Septuagint translates qahal by ekklēsia, the gathering of the people. Stephen speaks of Moses as "in the assembly in the wilderness" (Acts 7:38; KJV, "the church in the wilderness"). Hebrews 12:23 speaks of "the assembly of the firstborn." So the Christian word "church" goes back in part to Israel gathered at Horeb to hear God's voice. In Jewish tradition the day of the giving of the Torah is celebrated at the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot).

a: Your people whom you brought out of Egypt
p: God calls Israel Moses' people. Moses answers that they are God's people (9:26, 29).
b: The wording follows Exodus 32:7: "Your people, whom you brought up from the land of Egypt, have ruined themselves." God seems to disown Israel and hand them to Moses. In his prayer Moses turns the words back: "your people, your inheritance, whom you ransomed... and brought out of Egypt" (9:26) and "they are your people, your inheritance, whom you brought out" (9:29). The rabbis enjoyed the exchange as a model of bold prayer: Moses would not let God give up his claim.

a: Let go of me, so I can destroy them
p: God tells Moses to let go, as if Moses were holding him back. The Talmud found here an invitation to pray.
b: The Hebrew heref mimmenni means "let go of me, leave me be." In Exodus 32:10 the LORD uses a different verb with the same sense. The Talmud says that if the verse were not written, it could not be said: Moses took hold of God like a man who grabs his friend by his garment and says, "I will not let you go until you forgive them" (Bavli Berakhot 32a). God's words are read as an opening: he tells Moses what he will do if Moses does not stand in the way, and Moses stands in the way. Psalm 106:23 says Moses "stood in the broken wall facing him."

a: I smashed them in front of your eyes.
p: Moses' act may be anger, or a legal act: in the ancient Near East, breaking a tablet canceled a contract.
b: Exodus 32:19 says Moses' anger burned and he threw the tablets down. Deuteronomy adds that he did it "in front of your eyes," as a public act. In Mesopotamian law, to "break the tablet" (Akkadian tuppam hepû) meant to cancel the agreement written on it. Many scholars think Moses' act declared the covenant broken: Israel had violated its first terms within weeks. The rabbis had another view: Moses broke them so that Israel would be judged as a people who had not yet received the law, like a bride who had not yet signed the marriage contract (a midrash in Exodus Rabbah). The new tablets of 10:1–5 mark the covenant renewed.

a: Then I threw myself down before the LORD, as I had the first time
p: Exodus has Moses pray before going down and again afterward. Deuteronomy groups the events by theme.
b: In Exodus, Moses pleads on the mountain before he goes down (Exodus 32:11–14), breaks the tablets, destroys the calf, then goes up to seek forgiveness (32:30–34), and later stays forty days for the new tablets (34:28). Deuteronomy tells the breaking first, then a forty-day prayer, then the calf's destruction (9:21), and gives the words of the prayer only at the end (9:25–29). Traditional readers take Deuteronomy as a sermon that arranges memories for effect, not a timeline. Critical scholars see Deuteronomy drawing on the Exodus story, or both on an older account. The point of Deuteronomy's order is clear: Israel survived only because Moses prayed.

a: For I was afraid
p: Hebrews 12:21 borrows Moses' words from this verse, but sets them at the giving of the law rather than after the calf.
b: In the Septuagint Moses says here, "I am terrified" (ekphobos eimi). Hebrews 12:21 quotes it, adding "and trembling": "So terrifying was the sight that Moses said, 'I am terrified and trembling'" (a translation made for this note). In Deuteronomy Moses is afraid of God's anger at the golden calf, not of the fire at Sinai. Hebrews uses his words to sum up the terror of the mountain, and contrasts it with the joyful gathering at Mount Zion that Christians have come to (Hebrews 12:18–24). Readers have taken this as a free combination of scenes from the same forty days, typical of how Hebrews uses the Greek Bible.

a: The LORD was very angry with Aaron too, ready to destroy him.
p: Only Deuteronomy says Aaron's life was in danger and that Moses prayed for him.
b: Exodus 32 describes Aaron's part in making the calf, and his excuse, "I threw it in the fire, and out came this calf!" (Exodus 32:24), but not God's anger against him. Deuteronomy adds that Aaron too was in danger of death and was saved by his brother's prayer. Aaron later served as priest, and his death is noted in 10:6. The rabbis said Moses' prayer saved two of Aaron's four sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, while Nadab and Abihu died (Leviticus Rabbah 10:5).

a: Then I took the sinful thing you had made, the calf, and burned it in the fire.
p: The way the calf was destroyed matches a scene in the Canaanite myths of Ugarit, where the goddess Anat destroys the god Mot.
b: Moses burns, crushes, grinds and scatters the calf. In the Baal myth from Ugarit (about 1300 BC), the goddess Anat seizes Mot, god of death: "With a sword she split him, with a sieve she winnowed him, with fire she burned him, with millstones she ground him, in the field she scattered him." Samuel Loewenstamm showed that the Bible and the myth use a shared pattern for total destruction of a god. The link is real, but it is a common way of describing utter destruction, not a borrowing of the story. Exodus adds that Moses made the people drink the water (Exodus 32:20); Deuteronomy only says the dust went into the stream from the mountain. The calf is called "your sin," the thing that made Israel guilty.

a: At Taberah, at Massah and at Kibroth-hattaavah
p: Three short stories from Exodus and Numbers: a fire, a demand for water and a craving for meat.
b: Taberah, "Burning," was where "the LORD's fire had burned among them" when they complained (Numbers 11:1–3). Massah, "Testing," was where they demanded water (Exodus 17:1–7; see Deuteronomy 6:16). Kibroth-hattaavah, "Graves of Craving," was "because there they buried the people who had craved" meat (Numbers 11:34). Moses lists them out of order, as reminders of a pattern. The worst, the refusal at Kadesh, comes next (9:23).

a: Lord GOD, do not destroy your people, your inheritance
p: Moses' arguments are God's own people, God's promises and God's reputation. He never pleads Israel's goodness.
b: Moses' prayer (9:26–29) offers three reasons: Israel is God's people and inheritance, whom he redeemed; God promised Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; and the nations would say God failed or hated his people. It asks God to "not look at" their sin, but does not deny it. Exodus 32:11–13 and Numbers 14:13–19 give similar prayers. Many readers see here the model of intercession: appealing to God's character and commitments, not to the worth of those prayed for. Daniel 9:18 puts it this way: "not because of our righteous acts... but because of your great mercy."
r: 9:12; 9:29; Exodus 32:11–13; Numbers 14:13–19; Psalm 106:23; Daniel 9:15–19; Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25

a: Otherwise the people of the land you brought us out of will say
t: For the sake of God's name
p: Moses appeals to God's reputation among the nations. Ezekiel builds a whole theology on this.
b: The argument is that the exodus was public, so Israel's fate reflects on God. If they died in the desert, Egypt would say God could not finish what he started, or hated them. Joshua uses the same plea after the defeat at Ai (Joshua 7:9). Ezekiel 36:20–23 has God say he will act "for the sake of my holy name," which Israel had made unholy among the nations. Jesus teaches his followers to pray first, "may your name be honored as holy" (Matthew 6:9).

a: Also make yourself a wooden ark.
t: Who made the ark, and when?
p: Here Moses makes a plain wooden ark before the new tablets. In Exodus, Bezalel makes the gold-covered ark later.
b: Exodus 25:10–22 gives the plan for the ark, and Exodus 37:1 says, "Bezalel made the ark of acacia wood," covered with gold and topped by cherubim, after the second tablets. Deuteronomy has Moses make "an ark of acacia wood" himself, at once, and says nothing of gold or cherubim. Rashi and the Jerusalem Talmud solved this with two arks: Moses' simple box held the tablets until the tabernacle was built, and was later carried into battle, while Bezalel's stayed in the sanctuary. Many modern scholars see two traditions about the ark, with Deuteronomy's interested only in its role as a container for the covenant. The word aron means a chest or box.

a: which you smashed
p: The Talmud says God approved of Moses breaking the tablets. The broken pieces were kept in the ark too.
b: The Talmud lists the breaking of the tablets among three things Moses did on his own that God approved, and reads Exodus 34:1, "which you broke," as "well done for breaking them" (Bavli Shabbat 87a). Another tradition says that "the tablets and the fragments of the tablets were placed in the ark" (Bavli Bava Batra 14b; Berakhot 8b). The rabbis drew a lesson: treat an old scholar who has forgotten his learning with respect, as the broken tablets were kept beside the whole ones.

a: and they are still there
p: Deuteronomy says only the tablets. Kings agrees. Hebrews adds the jar of manna and Aaron's staff.
b: Deuteronomy's ark is a chest for the covenant document, as ancient treaties were kept in temples (see 4:13). 31:26 places the scroll of the law beside it. When Solomon brought the ark into the temple, "there was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets" (1 Kings 8:9, a translation made for this note). Hebrews 9:4 lists the golden jar of manna and Aaron's budding staff in it as well, following Exodus 16:33–34 and Numbers 17:10, which place them "before the testimony." The ark disappears from the record by the time of the Babylonian conquest; Jeremiah 3:16 says it will not be missed.
r: 31:26; Exodus 16:33–34; Exodus 25:16; Numbers 17:10; 1 Kings 8:9; Jeremiah 3:16; Hebrews 9:4

a: The Israelites set out from Beeroth Bene-jaakan to Moserah.
t: A fragment of a travel list
p: Verses 6–7 break into Moses' speech with stops on the journey. They differ from Numbers 33 in order and in where Aaron died.
b: The verses read like a piece of an itinerary. Numbers 33:30–33 lists "Moseroth," then "Bene-jaakan," then "Hor-haggidgad," then "Jotbathah," the reverse of the order here for the first two. Numbers 20:28 and 33:38 say Aaron died on Mount Hor, not at Moserah. Some readers take Moserah as the district around Mount Hor, and suggest Israel passed some places twice. Rashi says the people turned back eight stations in fear after Aaron's death. Critical scholars see an independent route list inserted here. The Samaritan Pentateuch rewrites the verses to agree with Numbers (see the variant). Why put this here? Perhaps to show that God did not destroy Aaron after the calf (9:20): he lived until his time and his son succeeded him.

a: At that time the LORD set apart the tribe of Levi
p: Here the whole tribe of Levi carries the ark, serves and blesses. Numbers keeps the priesthood for Aaron's sons.
b: "At that time" links Levi's choice to the calf, when the Levites rallied to Moses (Exodus 32:26–29). Deuteronomy often speaks of "the Levitical priests" (17:9; 18:1) and seems to allow any Levite to serve at the altar (18:6–8), while the priestly laws of Numbers sharply separate the priests, Aaron's descendants, from the other Levites, who carry and guard (Numbers 3–4; Numbers 18:1–7). Julius Wellhausen built part of his theory of the Torah's sources on this difference. Traditional readers explain that Deuteronomy uses "Levites" loosely and assumes the details known from Numbers. "To bless in his name" recalls the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:22–27).

a: The LORD is his inheritance
p: Levi gets no land; God is his portion. The church word "clergy" comes from the Greek for this "share."
b: God told Aaron, "I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites" (Numbers 18:20). Levi lived on the tithes and offerings (18:1–5) and in towns scattered among the tribes (Numbers 35:1–8). The psalmists apply the idea to anyone devoted to God: "The LORD is my portion" (Psalm 16:5; Psalm 73:26; Psalm 142:5). The Septuagint uses klēros, "lot, share," for Levi's inheritance, and Jerome explained the word "clergy" (clerici) from it: they are the Lord's lot, or the Lord is their lot (Letter 52).

a: what is the LORD your God asking from you?
p: The whole teaching summed up: fear, walk, love, serve, keep. Micah 6:8 asks the same question.
b: Moses gathers the book's key verbs into one sentence: fear God, walk in his ways, love him, serve him with all your heart and being, and keep his commands (10:12–13). Micah 6:8 echoes the form: "He has told you, human being, what is good. What does the LORD ask of you but to do justice, to love loyal love, and to walk humbly with your God?" (a translation made for this note). Jesus' summary of the law in the two great commands (Mark 12:29–31) follows the same instinct to state the heart of it all.

a: Only this: to fear the LORD your God
p: The Talmud took this verse to teach that everything is in God's hands except whether we fear him.
b: Rabbi Hanina said: "Everything is in the hands of heaven except the fear of heaven," and proved it from this verse: God "asks" for fear because it is the one thing he leaves to us (Bavli Berakhot 33b). The Talmud asks how fear can be called "only" a small thing, and answers: for Moses it was small. Another teacher read the Hebrew mah, "what," as me'ah, "a hundred," and taught that a person should say a hundred blessings every day (Bavli Menachot 43b).

a: even the highest heavens
p: The Hebrew "heavens of the heavens" means the highest heaven. Solomon says even it cannot contain God.
b: The Hebrew shemei ha-shamayim, "the heavens of the heavens," is a superlative: the heaven above all heavens. The verse sets God's ownership of everything against his choice of one small people (10:15): the God who owns the universe chose to love Israel's ancestors. Solomon uses the phrase at the temple's dedication: "the heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain you" (1 Kings 8:27, a translation made for this note). Psalm 148:4 calls on "you highest heavens" to praise. Paul speaks of being caught up "to the third heaven" (2 Corinthians 12:2).

a: So circumcise the foreskin of your heart
p: The sign on the body must be matched by a change inside. Later God promises to do it himself (30:6). Paul builds on it.
b: Circumcision was the sign of the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:10–14). Here it becomes a picture of the heart: cut away what makes it closed and stubborn, "and do not harden your neck any longer." The phrase "uncircumcised heart" appears in Leviticus 26:41, and Jeremiah 4:4 repeats this command. Deuteronomy 30:6 turns it into a promise: God himself will circumcise their hearts. The Dead Sea Scrolls use the image for the community's discipline (1QS 5:5). Paul writes that "circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter" (Romans 2:29), and Colossians 2:11 speaks of "a circumcision made without hands."
orig: וּמַלְתֶּם אֵת עָרְלַת לְבַבְכֶם (u-maltem et orlat levavkhem)
r: 30:6; Genesis 17:10–14; Leviticus 26:41; Jeremiah 4:4; Jeremiah 9:25–26; Romans 2:28–29; Colossians 2:11

a: the God of gods and the Lord of lords
t: God of gods, Lord of lords
p: A Hebrew way of saying "the supreme God, the supreme Lord." The title returns in the Psalms and in Revelation.
b: Like "heavens of heavens" (10:14), "God of gods" is a superlative. Psalm 136:2–3 uses both titles: "Give thanks to the God of gods... Give thanks to the Lord of lords." Daniel 2:47 has Nebuchadnezzar confess Daniel's God as "God of gods and Lord of kings." Revelation gives the Lamb the title "Lord of lords and King of kings" (Revelation 17:14; Revelation 19:16), and 1 Timothy 6:15 applies a similar title to God. In Deuteronomy the title leads into justice: this great God "does not play favorites" and cannot be bribed.

a: He sees that the orphan and the widow get justice. He loves the foreigner
p: Israel's care for the weak is grounded in God's own character: as he loves the foreigner, so must Israel (10:19).
b: Deuteronomy names three groups with no one to protect them: the orphan (literally "the fatherless"), the widow and the foreigner. God takes their side (10:18), so Israel must too (14:29; 16:11; 24:17–22; 27:19). The pattern "God does this, so you do it" is called imitatio Dei, the imitation of God. The Talmud's teaching that we cling to God by copying his acts of kindness (see 4:4) grows from texts like this. James 1:27 defines "religion pure and undefiled" as visiting "orphans and widows in their trouble."

a: So you are to love the foreigner, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.
p: Only here and in Leviticus 19:34 does the Bible command love for the foreigner. Memory of Egypt is the reason.
b: Leviticus 19:34 says: "The foreigner who lives with you is to be to you like one born among you. You are to love him as yourself, because you were foreigners in the land of Egypt." Deuteronomy gives a shorter version, but adds that God loves the foreigner first (10:18). The rabbis counted the command to love the foreigner among the most repeated in the Torah, and said that a convert must not be reminded of his past. Jesus' parable of the good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37) makes a foreigner the model of love for a neighbor.

a: He is your praise
p: The Hebrew tehillah can mean "the one you praise" or "your glory, what makes you famous."
b: Tehillatkha can mean the one Israel praises, the object of its song, or Israel's own fame and glory. 26:19 promises that God will set Israel high "for praise, for fame and for honor," and Jeremiah 17:14 says, "you are my praise." Both senses fit: the God Israel praises is also what gives Israel honor among the nations. The rest of the verse explains: he did the great and fearsome things Israel's own eyes saw.

a: Your ancestors went down to Egypt seventy persons in all.
p: The family that went to Egypt numbered seventy. Stephen in Acts says seventy-five, following the Greek of Genesis and Exodus.
b: Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 count the family of Jacob that came to Egypt as seventy. The Septuagint of those verses, and a Dead Sea Scroll of Exodus, give seventy-five, counting more of Joseph's descendants, and Stephen uses that figure (Acts 7:14). The contrast makes Moses' point: seventy became a nation as many as the stars of the sky (1:10). The verse also prepares for the confession of 26:5: "few in number" a people went down to Egypt and became a great nation there.

a: the training of the LORD your God
p: Musar means discipline or education. The plagues, the sea and the wilderness were God's schooling of Israel.
b: The word musar, from the verb in 8:5, covers both correction and instruction; in Proverbs it is the father's teaching (Proverbs 1:8). Moses lists the "lessons" Israel saw: the signs in Egypt, the drowning of the army, the wilderness, the death of Dathan and Abiram (11:3–6). The point is that Moses' hearers had seen it for themselves; their children had not, which is why they must teach them (11:19). Some readers note that most of the listeners were children at the time of the exodus, and take "you" as the people as a whole.

a: how he made the water of the Sea of Reeds flow over them as they chased you
p: Of all the exodus wonders, Moses picks the sea. Its result lasts "to this day."
b: Exodus tells how "the waters came back and covered the chariots and the horsemen, all Pharaoh's army that had gone into the sea after them. Not one of them was left" (Exodus 14:28). "To this day" probably means that Egypt's power to threaten Israel had been broken ever since. The sea crossing became the central picture of salvation in Israel's songs (Exodus 15; Psalm 106:9–12; Psalm 136:13–15) and in Christian teaching on baptism (1 Corinthians 10:1–2).
r: Exodus 14:21–31; Exodus 15:1–21; Joshua 24:6–7; Psalm 106:9–12; Psalm 136:13–15; 1 Corinthians 10:1–2

a: and what he did to Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, son of Reuben
p: Deuteronomy names only Dathan and Abiram, as does Psalm 106. Numbers 16 joins their revolt with Korah's.
b: Numbers 16:1 names "Korah son of Izhar... along with Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab." But the chapter tells of two groups: Korah's Levites, who want the priesthood and die by fire at the tent (Numbers 16:35), and the Reubenites Dathan and Abiram, who reject Moses' leadership and are swallowed by the earth (Numbers 16:31–33). Deuteronomy and Psalm 106:16–18 mention only Dathan and Abiram for the earth's swallowing. Many critical scholars see two stories woven together in Numbers 16, from different sources. Traditional readers note that Korah's sons did not die (Numbers 26:11), and that Moses here focuses on the rebels who denied his authority.

a: There you planted your seed and watered it with your foot, like a vegetable garden.
p: In Egypt, farmers watered from the Nile by hand and foot. In Canaan everything depends on rain.
b: Egypt gets almost no rain; its farms live on the yearly Nile flood and on canals. Farmers moved water into small plots by opening and closing earth channels with their feet, or by working water-lifting devices, such as the shaduf (a bucket on a pole) and later treadwheels. The rabbis and modern scholars both explain the phrase this way. The land of Canaan, by contrast, is hill country that "drinks water from the rain of the sky" (11:11). Moses presents this as an advantage and a test: Israel will depend each year on God's gift of rain, and so on its faithfulness (11:13–17).

a: It drinks water from the rain of the sky.
t: Rain from the LORD, not Baal
p: Canaanites thanked Baal, the storm god, for rain. Deuteronomy insists that the rain belongs to the LORD.
b: In the myths of Ugarit, Baal "gives his voice in the clouds" and sends rain; when he dies, the land dries up. For farmers in Canaan, rain was the great religious question. Deuteronomy answers it directly: the LORD gives "your land its rain at the right time" (11:14) and can "shut up the sky" (11:17). The contest between the LORD and Baal on Mount Carmel is a contest over rain (1 Kings 17:1; 1 Kings 18:1–45), and Hosea complains that Israel credited Baal with its grain, wine and oil (Hosea 2:8). The parallel with Baal is real and deliberate: the text claims for the LORD what Canaan gave Baal.

a: The eyes of the LORD your God are always on it, from the start of the year to the end of the year.
p: The rabbis read this verse as the source of the yearly judgment on the New Year: what the year will bring is decided at its start.
b: The verb darash means to seek, care for, look after. The land of Israel is pictured as under God's constant attention. The Talmud uses the verse to teach that at the New Year (Rosh Hashanah) it is decided what will happen at the end of the year, including the year's rain (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 8a, 16a). Rashi adds that God watches all lands, but through this one. The verse lies behind the Jewish idea of the land as specially holy.

a: If you truly listen to my commands that I am giving you today
t: The second paragraph of the Shema
p: 11:13–21 is said twice daily after 6:4–9. It speaks to the whole people, and promises reward and punishment.
b: The Mishnah calls the first paragraph of the Shema "accepting the yoke of the kingdom of heaven," and this second paragraph "accepting the yoke of the commands" (Mishnah Berakhot 2:2). It repeats much of 6:5–9 but in the plural "you," addressed to the community, and it adds rain and drought as the result of faithfulness or idolatry. Here Moses speaks in God's voice: "my commands," "I will give" (11:14–15). The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint keep Moses' voice: "he will give" (see the variant).

a: the early rain and the late rain
p: The first rains come in October and November and soften the ground for plowing. The last rains, in March and April, fill the grain.
b: The land of Israel has a dry summer and a rainy winter. The yoreh, the "early rain," comes in autumn and lets farmers plow and sow; the malqosh, the "late rain," comes in spring and ripens the wheat and barley before harvest. If either fails, the harvest fails. Jeremiah 5:24, Joel 2:23 and Hosea 6:3 use the pair, and James 5:7 compares patient faith to a farmer waiting "for the early and the late rain." The prayers for rain in the Jewish liturgy begin in autumn.

a: Watch yourselves, or your heart will be fooled.
p: The order of the verses is a warning: you will eat and be full (11:15), then watch out (11:16).
b: The Sifre notices the order and draws the lesson that people rebel when they are full, not when they are hungry, as with the generation of the flood and the men of Sodom. The verb pattah means to be lured or talked into something, as when Delilah lures Samson (Judges 16:5). The same warning appears in 6:10–12 and 8:12–14, and the song of Moses tells it as a story: "Jeshurun grew fat and kicked" (see 32:15).

a: He will shut up the sky, and there will be no rain.
p: Drought is the covenant's sign of God's anger. Solomon, Elijah and James all use the picture.
b: Solomon prays at the temple: "When the sky is shut and there is no rain because they have sinned against you" (1 Kings 8:35, a translation made for this note). Elijah announces a drought to King Ahab (1 Kings 17:1), and James 5:17 says Elijah prayed and "it did not rain on the earth for three years and six months." 28:23–24 develops the curse: a sky of bronze and ground of iron. Amos 4:7–8 lists drought among the warnings Israel ignored.

a: So put these words of mine on your heart and in your being.
p: Rashi, following the Sifre, read the repeat of 6:6–9 here as a command to keep the law even outside the land.
b: Because this paragraph follows the warning of being driven from the land (11:17), the Sifre and Rashi say it means: even when you are in exile, keep wearing tefillin and fixing mezuzot, so that they will not be new to you when you return. Jeremiah 31:21 is read the same way: "Set up road markers." Modern scholars note that the repetition of 6:6–9 frames the long section 6:4–11:21 as one unit, beginning and ending with the same words. See the notes on 6:8–9 for tefillin and the mezuzah.

a: as many as the days the sky is above the earth
p: A way of saying "forever," like the promise to David in Psalm 89.
b: The sky above the earth was the most lasting thing anyone could see. Psalm 89:29 promises David's line "his throne as the days of the heavens" (a translation made for this note), and Jeremiah 31:35–36 ties Israel's survival to the fixed order of sun, moon and stars. The promise here is conditional, set within a call to faithfulness, but its scale is endless. The rabbis also read the verse "to give them" (not "to you") as a hint of the resurrection: God swore to give the land to the ancestors themselves (Bavli Sanhedrin 90b).

a: Every place the sole of your foot steps on will be yours.
p: God repeats these words to Joshua as the conquest begins. The borders match 1:7.
b: Joshua 1:3–4 quotes the promise almost word for word as God's first words to Joshua after Moses' death. The borders are those of 1:7: from the southern wilderness to Lebanon, and from the Euphrates to "the western sea," the Mediterranean. Walking on land was a way of claiming it, as God told Abraham, "Get up and walk through the land, its length and its width" (Genesis 13:17). The promise has a condition in 11:22: keeping the whole command. Caleb received the land "his feet have walked on" (1:36).

a: a blessing and a curse
p: The second speech's introduction ends with a choice. Its laws will end the same way, with blessings and curses (chapters 27–28).
b: Chapters 6–11 urge love and loyalty; 12–26 give the laws; 27–28 give the blessings and curses. This verse previews the end. Ancient treaties also closed with blessings for loyalty and curses for betrayal, which is one reason many scholars read Deuteronomy against them. The same choice returns at the end of Moses' third speech, where he sets before Israel life and death (see 30:15–19). Jewish tradition stresses that the choice is real and human freedom genuine. Paul reads the curse in the light of Christ, who became "a curse for us" (Galatians 3:10–14).

a: to follow other gods you have not known
p: To "know" in Hebrew is to have a relationship. These gods have no history with Israel; they did nothing for it.
b: The phrase "other gods you have not known" (13:2, 6, 13; 28:64; 29:26; 32:17) contrasts with what Israel has known of the LORD: the exodus, the sea, the desert (11:2–7). To "know" here is to have experienced, as in Hosea 13:4: "You know no god but me" (a translation made for this note). The point is not that these gods were unheard of, but that Israel had no reason to trust them.

a: the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal
p: Two mountains face each other across the valley of Shechem. The ceremony is described in 27:11–26 and done in Joshua 8.
b: Mount Gerizim rises on the south side of the valley where Shechem (modern Nablus) lies, and Mount Ebal on the north. The pass between them is a natural amphitheater, and a voice can carry across it. 27:11–26 gives the rite, with tribes on each mountain, and Joshua 8:30–35 tells how it was carried out. Gerizim later became the Samaritans' holy mountain, where they still celebrate Passover. On Mount Ebal, Adam Zertal excavated a stone structure from about 1200 BC that he identified as Joshua's altar; others think it was a farm or watchtower.

a: beside the great trees of Moreh
p: The place where God first appeared to Abraham in Canaan. The mention of Gilgal here is puzzling.
b: Genesis 12:6 says Abram came "as far as the place at Shechem, the great tree of Moreh." Moreh may mean "teacher," perhaps a tree where oracles were given. Israel will begin its life in the land where Abraham began his. "Across from Gilgal" is hard: the well-known Gilgal is near Jericho, some 30 miles away. Some think another Gilgal lay near Shechem; others take the phrase loosely. The Samaritan Pentateuch adds "across from Shechem" (see the variant). The question of where the place the LORD would choose (12:5) was, Jerusalem or Gerizim, later divided Jews and Samaritans.
r: Genesis 12:6–7; Genesis 35:4; Joshua 4:19; Joshua 24:26; Judges 9:37; John 4:20

a: be careful to do all the rules and the rulings I am setting before you today
p: The long introduction ends here. The laws themselves begin with 12:1, which repeats "rules and rulings."
b: Chapters 5–11 urge Israel to love and obey; 12:1 begins the laws with the words "These are the rules and the rulings." Many critical scholars think the law code of chapters 12–26 is the oldest core of the book, perhaps the scroll found in the temple under King Josiah (2 Kings 22–23), and that chapters 5–11 were written as a preface. Traditional readers see a speech built like a sermon: first the heart (love the LORD), then the details. Either way, the order teaches that the laws flow from a relationship.
